title.rendered: ePlanet Brokers Publishes H1 2026 Transparency Report and Highlights Best Broker 2026 Award

content.rendered:
Dubai, UAE, October 7th, 2026, FinanceWire

ePlanet Brokers has published its H1 2026 Transparency Report, providing operational data on withdrawals, deposits, KYC, trading execution and customer support. The publication comes alongside another development for the company in 2026: ePlanet Brokers received the Best Broker 2026 award at Forex Expo Dubai 2026. Together, these developments provide additional information for traders researching the broker and asking questions such as: Is ePlanet Brokers legit? Is ePlanet Brokers safe to use?

Choosing a broker is rarely about one feature, award or performance figure. A useful review needs to look at legal structure, operational data, withdrawals, execution, support and the problems a broker is willing to disclose. That is the context behind the ePlanet Brokers H1 2026 Transparency Report. Instead of relying only on claims such as “fast” or “reliable,” the company published internal performance figures covering several stages of the client journey.

Transparency Report Findings

Some of the clearest numbers relate to payments and trading operations. During H1 2026, ePlanet Brokers reported a 99% deposit success rate and a withdrawal success rate of more than 95%. Average internal withdrawal processing time was approximately eight minutes.

Bank processing, payment providers, verification or compliance checks can affect how long a withdrawal ultimately takes.

The report also says more than 40% of withdrawals were automated. At the same time, it does not present withdrawals as problem-free. It identifies interbank processing, bank-specific restrictions and additional reviews among reasons a request may take longer.

Trading data provides another useful measure. ePlanet Brokers reported a 99.9% order execution success rate and average execution speed of approximately 110 milliseconds, compared with around 150 milliseconds in H2 2025. These are aggregate figures rather than a promise that every order will have the same result or execution time.

The report is useful because it does not only highlight positive results. It also explains where delays can happen and where further improvement is planned. That matters in a broker review: transparency is more useful when readers can see both reported performance and the operational limits behind the headline numbers.

KYC and Customer Support

KYC is another area where the report includes both performance and friction. The published approval rate is 88%, while automated identity verification averaged less than 30 seconds. The report also discusses issues that can slow verification, including incomplete or unclear documentation and cases requiring additional checks.

Support performance is measured as well. Average first response time was 181 seconds, while average resolution time was 67 minutes. This approach is relevant when assessing whether ePlanet Brokers is safe or legit. No operational metric can prove that a broker is risk-free, and trading itself carries substantial risk. But measurable data can make it easier to examine how a company operates and where its processes still need work.

How is ePlanet Brokers structured?

ePlanet Brokers operates through entities in more than one jurisdiction.

ePlanet Brokers LTD is incorporated and registered in the Comoros Union under the International Companies Act 2006, with IBC Registration No. HY00923038. Nebula Ventures Ltd is incorporated in Vanuatu under Company Registration No. 700819 and is licensed and regulated by the Vanuatu Financial Services Commission to provide financial dealer services.

The Vanuatu entity was added alongside the existing Comoros structure rather than replacing it. For traders reviewing whether ePlanet Brokers is a legitimate broker, these details should be considered together with the company’s terms, risk disclosures and operational record.

Best Broker 2026 Award

ePlanet Brokers also received the Best Broker 2026 award at Forex Expo Dubai 2026. An industry award is useful context, but it should not replace due diligence. The company makes the same point in its own coverage of the award: traders should still examine legal information, trading conditions, platforms and operational performance.

One is industry recognition; the other provides numbers that can be checked and compared over time.

ePlanet Brokers Review 2026

The strongest part of this ePlanet Brokers review is not a claim that every process is perfect. It is the availability of measurable information, including areas where delays or additional checks can occur.

For anyone asking whether ePlanet Brokers is safe or legit, there is no single metric that should decide the answer. Regulation, withdrawal performance, execution, support, legal documents and risk all matter. The H1 2026 Transparency Report adds another layer by making operational results visible, while the Best Broker 2026 award adds external industry recognition.

Together, they give traders more information to examine before making their own decision.

About ePlanet Brokers

ePlanet Brokers is a global online broker providing access to financial markets through MetaTrader 5 and cTrader. The company operates through entities established in multiple jurisdictions, including the Comoros Union and Vanuatu, and provides trading services across a range of financial instruments. ePlanet Brokers focuses on trading technology, operational transparency and multilingual client support, while continuing to develop its trading infrastructure and client services.

title.rendered: Hadrian, Interview With CEO Rogier Fischer

content.rendered:
Some days ago, Hadrian, an Amsterdam, The Netherlands-based provider of an agentic AI offensive security platform, raised $40M in funding. In conjunction with the announcement, CEO Rogier Fischer joined us to participate in our Q&A.

Hi Rogier, can you tell us a bit more about yourself? What’s your background?

I started hacking when I was 12. By my mid-teens I was reporting security flaws to Dutch banks and to companies like Google, Microsoft, and Yahoo, which list me in their security halls of fame. Before Hadrian, I co-founded the crypto trading platform LiteBit and was its CTO. We grew it past $750 million in trading volume.

I founded Hadrian in Amsterdam in 2021 with Olivier Beg and Maurice Clin. I met Olivier on a hacking forum in 2009, and Maurice and I studied together at London Business School. Olivier and I had spent years testing companies by hand, and we started Hadrian to automate that work.

Let’s speak about Hadrian. What is the market problem you want to solve? What is the real opportunity?

Companies change what they have on the internet every day as they ship new code and set up new cloud services, and more of that code is now written with AI. Most companies still check whether any of it can be attacked with a penetration test, done by people, once or twice a year. They ship changes orders of magnitude faster than they test them.

Attackers scan continuously, and they now use AI to find and exploit weaknesses faster than before. Our own data shows companies are typically unaware of 30 to 40% of their internet-facing assets, so nobody is testing those systems.

We want companies to test as often as they change. Security teams already have budget for pentesting. We think AI will do nearly all of that testing, with people deciding what gets tested and fixing what is found.

What are the features differentiating the product from competitors?

Hadrian has two products:

  1. Atlas continuously maps a company’s external attack surface, including assets the security team doesn’t know about. 
  2. Nova is our agentic pentester that tests whether the exposures Atlas finds can be exploited and chains them into the attack paths a real attacker would use. 

Nova’s findings also go back into Atlas, so both products work from the same data.

Most security tools produce long lists of possible issues, and teams spend their time working out which ones matter. Hadrian shows which exposures an attacker could actually use, with evidence. Our team also includes a lot of hackers. Around 10 to 15% of our people come from ethical hacking, and our AI agents use their methods.

You just raised a new funding round. Please, tell us more about it.

We’ve raised $40 million in a Series B co-led by Forgepoint Capital International and Smartfin, with participation from HV Capital, Motive Partners, Picus Capital, and Oetker Ventures. Damien Henault, Managing Director and Partner at Forgepoint Capital International, is joining our board. He has backed several companies in exposure management and knows this market well.

We’ll spend the money on engineering and research for autonomous testing, so Nova can take on more of the work pentesters do today, and on building teams in the US and across Europe.

Can you share some numbers and achievements for the business?

More than 1000 companies use Hadrian today, including Visma, McKesson, Crédit Agricole, Amadeus, and Francisco Partners. They include banks, manufacturers, healthcare companies, and private equity firms. We’ve grown to about 90 people.

Frost & Sullivan and GigaOm have recognized Hadrian as a leader, and we’re included in Gartner Market Guides. We hold SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications, which enterprises ask for before they let AI agents test their production systems. Our research team also releases free tools for the security community, including OpenHack, SubWiz, and SanicDNS.

What are your medium-term plans?

We want continuous autonomous testing to become the normal way companies check their security. For the product, that means Nova doing more of the work end to end and covering more types of systems, while people stay in charge of scope and remediation. I believe AI will do nearly all offensive security testing in the near future, and we’re building Hadrian for that.

We’re also expanding in the US and continuing to grow across Europe. We’ll keep hiring engineers and researchers, many with hacking backgrounds, because our AI agents learn how attackers work from them.

title.rendered: 10 HR Tech Tools Helping Startups Scale Their People Operations in 2026

content.rendered:
When your startup has ten employees, HR can feel manageable from a shared spreadsheet and a handful of folders.

Once you start hiring rapidly, however, employee records, onboarding, payroll, time off, performance reviews and compliance create a much larger workload. That shift matters across the US economy, with small firms accounting for 51% of net job creation from the third quarter of 2020 through the third quarter of 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Why HR software matters as you grow

The right HR software for growing companies gives you a structured place to manage recurring people processes, so your team can spend less time chasing paperwork and more time supporting employees. Modern platforms can connect employee records with onboarding, time off, recruiting, performance and reporting, becoming increasingly useful as headcount rises. Lattice’s 2026 research found that 25% of surveyed HR teams prioritize updating HR technology, showing how software remains a practical concern for people teams.

1. TalentHR

In pole position, TalentHR gives growing startups a broad collection of everyday HR tools without requiring a complicated setup. You can manage employee records, time off, documents, onboarding, benefits, performance, goals, time tracking and surveys from one platform, so you have fewer disconnected processes to monitor. Its current pricing includes a free plan for up to 10 users, with paid plans starting at $2 per user per month, suiting a startup building its HR foundation.

2. Gusto

Gusto brings HR administration together with payroll, benefits and employee management, so you can handle several important responsibilities through one system. Its current tools cover recruiting, onboarding checklists, document storage, electronic signatures, time tracking, performance reviews and goal setting, with international contractor payments available across more than 120 countries. For a US startup, that combination can make everyday administration easier to organize as your workforce grows beyond its earliest stage.

3. Rippling

Rippling focuses on keeping employee information connected across HR processes, so a change to someone’s manager, department or employment details can flow through the relevant systems. Its HR platform currently supports onboarding, document management, time off, employee self-service, reporting and compliance across all 50 states and more than 180 countries. If your startup has several HR workflows running simultaneously, that connected structure can reduce repetitive administrative work as your headcount increases.

4. Deel

Deel is built with international teams in mind, so it becomes relevant when your startup hires employees or contractors across borders. Its HRIS brings employee records, onboarding, offboarding, time off, documents, workflows and people analytics together, with support for EOR employees, direct employees and contractors in more than 150 countries. That reach can give you a consistent administrative framework as your company expands into new markets and your workforce becomes geographically distributed.

5. BambooHR

BambooHR covers a wide portion of the employee lifecycle, so you can manage areas such as HR data, recruiting, onboarding, payroll, benefits, time and attendance, performance, compensation and compliance from one platform. That breadth can become useful once your startup has enough employees for separate HR tasks to compete for your attention every week. You can also connect workforce information across different functions, keeping employee records organized as your company develops.

6. Workable

Workable puts recruiting and people management into one platform, so it can be useful when hiring becomes one of your biggest operational priorities. Its current features include distribution across more than 200 job boards, candidate management, onboarding, employee profiles, time off and reporting, with more than 270 integrations available. If you are moving from occasional founder-led hiring toward repeatable recruitment, having candidate and employee workflows connected can make the transition easier to manage.

7. Lattice

Lattice focuses heavily on performance, engagement and employee development, so it fits startups that are building more structured management practices. Its 2026 research found that 40% of surveyed HR professionals ranked performance management as a top priority, with employee engagement close behind at 39%. You can use Lattice for performance reviews, goals, feedback and related people processes, giving managers a clearer framework for regular conversations as teams become larger.

8. HiBob

HiBob provides HR tools covering employee information, onboarding, time off, performance, compensation, engagement and reporting, so you can centralize many routine people processes as your startup expands. That becomes useful when several departments begin maintaining their own information and managers need consistent access to workforce data. For a growing company, the value comes from creating repeatable processes that employees and managers can follow, making everyday HR administration easier to coordinate across teams.

9. Paycor

Paycor combines payroll with HR and workforce management capabilities, so it can give growing US businesses a broader system for handling employee administration. Its platform covers areas such as payroll, recruiting, onboarding, time tracking, benefits and talent management, meaning you can connect several recurring responsibilities through one provider. If your startup is moving toward more formal HR processes, having payroll and workforce information together can simplify the way you manage routine employee tasks.

10. TriNet

TriNet combines HR technology with payroll, benefits and workforce services, so it offers startups another way to organize people administration as employment responsibilities become more complex. Its services cover areas such as payroll, benefits, time tracking and onboarding, with additional HR support available alongside the technology. For you as a founder or small HR team, that combination can provide a practical framework for managing routine processes as your company adds employees, departments and new responsibilities.

title.rendered: The Role of Data Analysis in Modern Investment Decision-Making

content.rendered:
Modern investing is no longer driven only by instinct, headlines, or a single “hot tip.” Investors now have access to company filings, market prices, economic indicators, portfolio dashboards, and behavioral signals that can turn uncertainty into a more structured decision-making process.

This helps individuals and organizations evaluate risk, compare opportunities, and measure whether their strategy is actually working.

Why does data matter so much in investing?

Data matters because every investment decision involves incomplete information, and analysis helps reduce the amount of guesswork involved. It cannot predict the future with certainty, but it can reveal patterns, test assumptions, and show whether an opportunity aligns with an investor’s goals, timeline, and risk tolerance. In practical terms, data analysis in investment turns scattered information into a clearer view of what is happening, what could happen next, and what trade-offs are involved.

Without data, investors may overreact to short-term noise, follow emotional narratives, or hold positions for reasons that no longer make sense. With data, they can compare assets more consistently, review past decisions more honestly, and avoid relying on memory alone. This is especially important in fast-moving markets, where prices can change quickly and sentiment can shift before the underlying fundamentals do.

The core types of data investors use

Financial data analysis begins with understanding which data points are useful and why they matter. Not every number deserves equal attention. A thoughtful investor looks for information that connects directly to value, risk, liquidity, growth, income, or market behavior.

Common data categories include:

  • Fundamental data: Revenue, earnings, cash flow, debt, margins, dividends, and valuation ratios help investors understand the financial health of a company or asset.
  • Market data: Prices, trading volume, volatility, bid-ask spreads, and price trends show how buyers and sellers are behaving in real time.
  • Economic data: Interest rates, inflation, employment, consumer spending, and GDP trends provide context for broader market conditions.
  • Portfolio data: Allocation, concentration, drawdowns, correlation, and return history help investors see how individual holdings work together.
  • Qualitative data: Management commentary, competitive positioning, regulatory changes, and industry trends add context that numbers alone may not capture.

The value comes from combining these inputs rather than treating one metric as a complete answer. A stock may look inexpensive based on valuation, for example, but weak cash flow, high debt, or deteriorating industry conditions may tell a more cautious story.

Data transforms opinions into testable assumptions

One of the biggest benefits of investment analysis is discipline. Instead of saying, “This company looks promising,” an investor can define what would make that view true or false. That might include revenue growth, improving margins, stronger free cash flow, or price behavior that confirms market support.

This shift matters because markets often reward patience, but they also punish stubbornness. Data helps investors distinguish between a temporary setback and a broken thesis. If the reason for owning an investment changes, the decision should be reviewed with the same seriousness as the original purchase.

A simple decision framework can help:

  1. Define the investment thesis. Clarify why the asset is attractive and what outcome you expect.
  2. Identify the key metrics. Choose the data points that would confirm or challenge that thesis.
  3. Set review intervals. Decide when to revisit the position rather than reacting every time the price moves.
  4. Compare alternatives. Ask whether capital could be better used elsewhere.
  5. Document the decision. Record the reasoning so future reviews are based on facts, not hindsight.

This process does not remove uncertainty. It simply makes uncertainty easier to manage.

What investment performance metrics should investors track?

Investment performance metrics should show not only how much money an investment made or lost, but also how much risk was taken to achieve that result. Total return is important, but it is only the beginning. Investors also need to evaluate consistency, volatility, downside risk, and whether the performance fits the purpose of the portfolio.

Useful metrics often include:

  • Total return: Measures price appreciation plus income, such as dividends or interest.
  • Annualized return: Converts performance into a yearly rate, making it easier to compare investments over different time periods.
  • Volatility: Shows how much returns fluctuate, which can affect both risk and investor behavior.
  • Maximum drawdown: Measures the largest peak-to-trough decline, helping investors understand potential downside.
  • Sharpe ratio or risk-adjusted return: Compares return to the level of risk taken.
  • Benchmark comparison: Evaluates whether an investment or portfolio is outperforming a relevant market index or peer group.

These metrics are most useful when matched to the investor’s objective. A retiree seeking income may care more about stability and cash flow, while a long-term growth investor may accept more volatility for higher potential returns. The right metric depends on the job the investment is supposed to do.

Charts add context to market behavior

Numbers from financial statements can explain business quality, but price charts can show how the market is responding. Technical tools such as moving averages, support and resistance levels, trendlines, and volume patterns can help investors identify momentum, weakness, or possible turning points. These tools are not magic signals, but they can add useful timing and risk-management context.

For investors who want to better understand visual market signals, resources focused on stock chart analysis can support a more informed approach to evaluating price trends. Chart analysis is often most effective when paired with fundamental research, because a strong business can still be poorly timed, and a rising chart can still mask weak underlying fundamentals.

The goal is not to stare at every price movement. It is to understand whether market behavior supports or contradicts the broader investment case.

Data helps manage risk before losses become emotional

Risk management is one of the most practical uses of data analysis in investment. Investors often discover too late that their portfolio is overly concentrated in one sector, dependent on a single economic outcome, or exposed to assets that tend to fall at the same time. Portfolio-level data makes these risks visible before they become painful.

Important risk questions include:

  • Are too many holdings influenced by the same interest-rate, currency, or commodity trend?
  • Does one position account for an outsized share of portfolio performance?
  • How has the portfolio behaved during previous market declines?
  • Are income needs, time horizon, and liquidity requirements reflected in the allocation?
  • Would a sudden decline force selling at an unfavorable time?

These questions help investors move beyond simply asking, “What should I buy?” A better question is, “What role should this investment play, and what risk does it add?”

Human judgment still matters

Data is powerful, but it is not a substitute for judgment. Models can be built on flawed assumptions, historical patterns can break, and clean-looking dashboards can create false confidence. Investors must still interpret the information, question the source, and recognize that markets are influenced by people, policy, competition, and unexpected events.

The best decisions usually combine evidence with humility. Data can highlight opportunities, but it should also reveal what is unknown. A disciplined investor uses analysis to prepare for multiple outcomes rather than pretending there is only one possible future.

It is also important to avoid analysis paralysis. More data does not always mean better insight. After a certain point, adding another metric may delay action without improving the decision. The key is to focus on information that changes what you would actually do.

A practical takeaway for modern investors

Financial data analysis gives investors a clearer, more repeatable way to make decisions. It helps define goals, compare opportunities, evaluate risk, and measure results through relevant investment performance metrics. Whether reviewing a single stock, a diversified portfolio, or a long-term strategy, data provides a foundation for better questions and more disciplined choices.

Modern investing will always involve uncertainty. But investors who use data thoughtfully are better equipped to separate signal from noise, manage emotions, and adapt when conditions change. The goal is not perfect prediction; it is making better decisions with the information available.

title.rendered: Why Enterprise Companies Need More Than an In-House SEO Team

content.rendered:
Enterprise SEO is too large, too cross-functional, and too fast-moving to rely on one internal team alone.

An in-house SEO team is essential because it understands the brand, products, approval process, and business goals, but enterprise growth often requires extra strategy, outside perspective, technical depth, and execution support. The strongest enterprise seo strategies usually combine internal expertise with specialized external partners who can help teams move faster and make better decisions.

Why is an in-house SEO team not always enough?

An in-house SEO team is not always enough because enterprise websites are complex systems, not simple marketing channels. Large companies often manage thousands of pages, multiple product lines, regional sites, legacy platforms, long approval chains, and competing priorities across departments. Even talented SEO professionals can struggle to cover technical audits, content planning, reporting, stakeholder education, experimentation, competitive analysis, and implementation follow-up at the same time.

This does not mean the internal team is failing. In many cases, the opposite is true: the team sees what needs to happen but lacks the time, access, or specialized support to push every initiative forward. SEO at enterprise scale depends on collaboration with developers, content teams, legal reviewers, brand managers, analytics teams, and executives. When any part of that chain slows down, progress can stall.

Outside support can fill the gaps without replacing internal ownership. A partner can bring added capacity, fresh perspective, and focused expertise while the in-house team continues to guide priorities and protect brand standards.

Enterprise SEO requires more than daily optimization

For smaller websites, seo optimization may focus on improving pages, publishing helpful content, and fixing obvious technical issues. Enterprise SEO includes those tasks, but the work is broader. A single recommendation can affect hundreds or thousands of URLs, multiple templates, and several business units.

That scale makes planning more important than quick fixes. Teams need to understand which changes will create the most value, which risks need attention first, and which projects require coordination across departments. Without a clear operating model, SEO becomes reactive: one team asks for content, another requests reporting, and technical issues get handled only when they become urgent.

Effective enterprise seo strategies connect SEO work to business priorities. They help teams decide where to invest effort, how to measure progress, and how to explain SEO decisions in language that non-specialists understand.

The common limits of relying only on internal resources

Even well-funded companies face practical constraints. Internal SEO teams are often pulled into meetings, urgent launches, reporting requests, and last-minute reviews. That leaves less time for deep analysis or long-term planning.

Common challenges include:

  • Limited bandwidth: Internal teams may know what should be done but cannot execute or manage every project at once.
  • Specialized technical needs: Large sites often require advanced crawling, indexing, migration, structured data, and site architecture support.
  • Content scale: Creating, refreshing, and governing content across many pages requires planning, workflows, and quality control.
  • Internal politics: SEO recommendations can compete with design, legal, product, or engineering priorities.
  • Tool and data overload: Enterprises often have plenty of data but not enough time to translate it into clear action.
  • Blind spots: Teams working inside the same company every day may miss patterns an outside specialist would notice quickly.

These problems are rarely solved by simply asking the in-house team to “do more.” More work without more support can lead to slower projects, missed opportunities, and employee burnout.

What outside SEO support adds to the team

Hiring an enterprise SEO agency works best when it strengthens the internal team rather than taking control away from it. A good partner can help clarify priorities, bring proven processes, and support work that requires extra hands or specialized experience.

For example, an outside team may help audit a large site before a redesign, review technical risks during a platform migration, or build a content roadmap for multiple product categories. They can also provide independent analysis when leadership needs confidence before investing in a major SEO initiative.

This outside perspective is especially useful because enterprise companies can become used to their own systems. A partner can ask simple but important questions: Are the most valuable pages easy to find? Are teams duplicating content efforts? Are technical issues preventing useful pages from being discovered? Are reports showing business impact clearly enough for decision-makers?

Strong SEO strategies depend on cross-functional alignment

Enterprise SEO succeeds when departments understand how their work affects search visibility and user experience. Developers influence site performance and crawlability. Content teams shape what users learn. Product teams affect page structure and messaging. Executives influence budget, timelines, and priorities.

Because of this, SEO cannot sit in a corner as a purely marketing function. It needs shared ownership. The in-house team is usually best positioned to build relationships across the company, while an external partner can support that effort with documentation, training, audits, and clear recommendations.

A practical alignment plan might include:

  1. Define SEO goals in business terms. Connect projects to revenue, lead quality, customer education, brand visibility, or operational efficiency.
  2. Create clear decision rules. Decide which SEO issues are urgent, which can wait, and who approves changes.
  3. Build repeatable workflows. Add SEO review points to launches, redesigns, migrations, and content planning.
  4. Use simple reporting. Show what changed, why it matters, and what should happen next.
  5. Educate key teams. Help non-SEO colleagues understand the basics without overwhelming them with jargon.

When alignment improves, SEO becomes less of a last-minute checklist and more of a normal part of how the company builds digital experiences.

How should enterprise companies combine internal and external SEO?

Enterprise companies should combine internal and external SEO by keeping strategy ownership inside the business while using outside support for specialized expertise, scale, and momentum. The in-house team should set priorities, manage relationships, and ensure all recommendations fit the company’s goals. External partners should bring structure, analysis, and execution support where internal resources are stretched.

This model works because both sides bring something different. Internal teams understand the brand, customers, politics, and long-term roadmap. External teams often bring experience from multiple industries, broader pattern recognition, and focused time for projects that internal teams cannot fully own.

The best partnerships are collaborative, not transactional. Instead of sending a long list of disconnected recommendations, a strong partner helps the company decide what matters most and how to get it done.

Signs your enterprise SEO model needs extra support

A company may need more than its current in-house setup if SEO projects regularly start but do not finish. Another sign is when reporting exists, but leaders still do not understand what actions to take. If technical fixes sit in development queues for months, content updates happen inconsistently, or major site changes launch without SEO review, the operating model may need reinforcement.

It is also worth seeking support when the business is entering a period of change. Website redesigns, international expansion, mergers, rebrands, CMS changes, and product launches can all create SEO risks and opportunities. Bringing in added expertise before these projects begin is usually more effective than trying to repair problems after launch.

A balanced approach creates better long-term results

The question is not whether enterprise companies should choose internal or external SEO. The better question is how to build a model where both work together. An in-house team provides continuity, context, and accountability. External support adds depth, speed, and perspective.

When those roles are clear, SEO becomes easier to manage across a large organization. Teams can focus on the right priorities, avoid preventable mistakes, and create digital experiences that are easier for people to find and use.

Enterprise SEO is a long-term discipline, not a one-time project. Companies that treat it as a shared, supported business function are better positioned to adapt, improve, and grow without placing the entire burden on one internal team.

title.rendered: Enterprise Reputation Management in the Age of AI: Protecting Hundreds of Locations at Once

content.rendered:
Someone in Tampa opens ChatGPT at 9 p.m. and types: “best gym near me that’s open late and doesn’t have billing issues.”

The answer names two competitors and one of your locations. It’s the one with a 3.6 rating and eleven unanswered reviews about cancellation fees. Your other six Tampa locations, all rated 4.6 or higher, don’t appear at all.

Nobody at headquarters will ever see that answer. There’s no ranking report for it and no position to track. The customer just goes somewhere else.

That’s what franchise reputation management looks like in 2026. The brand is only as trusted as whatever the AI decides to say about it, and the AI is reading every location, not just the flagship.

What is enterprise reputation management?

Enterprise reputation management is the practice of monitoring, protecting, and improving how a multi-location brand is perceived across every location, review platform, search result, and AI assistant at the same time. Franchise reputation management is the same discipline with one complication: the brand owns the name, but independent franchisees run the daily operations that generate reviews.

For a brand with 300 locations, that means 300 Google Business Profiles, 300 review streams, 300 sets of hours and phone numbers, and 300 managers who may or may not answer a one-star review this month. AI assistants now pull from all of it when they decide who to recommend.

AI is a far pickier gatekeeper than Google

Google’s local pack was never easy, but it was generous compared to what came next.

SOCi’s 2026 Local Visibility Index analyzed 2,751 multi-location brands across roughly 350,000 locations. Brands showed up in Google’s local 3-pack 35.9% of the time. ChatGPT recommended just 1.2% of locations. Gemini recommended 11%.

Read that ChatGPT number again. For every 100 locations a brand operates, ChatGPT surfaces about one.

The locations that did get recommended weren’t random. They averaged 4.3 stars on ChatGPT and 4.2 on Perplexity. Meanwhile, the average Google review response rate across the study was 46.9%, which means more than half of all reviews at these brands never got a reply. On Yelp, the response rate was 3.1%.

So the bar went up, and most enterprise brands are still clearing the old one.

Your customers already switched tools

This isn’t a forecast. BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey of 1,002 U.S. adults found 45% of consumers now use AI tools for local business recommendations, up from 6% a year earlier. Google’s share of review readers dropped from 83% to 71% over the same period.

Consumer standards tightened at the same time:

  • 31% will only consider a business rated 4.5 stars or higher, up from 17% in 2025
  • 68% require at least 4 stars
  • 74% want reviews written in the last three months, and 32% want them from the last two weeks
  • 19% expect a same-day response to a review, up from 6%
  • 50% say a generic, templated response makes them unlikely to choose the business

One more number worth keeping in mind: 97% of AI users say they double-check recommendations against real reviews on the native platform. AI builds the shortlist. Your reviews still close the deal. You need both.

The weakest location writes the brand’s story

Most enterprise dashboards lead with a brand-wide average rating. That number is close to useless now.

A 4.4 average can hide 40 locations sitting at 3.5. When a customer asks an AI tool about a specific city, it won’t average you out. It’ll pick the location nearest the query and describe it honestly. When someone asks about the brand itself (“is [brand] any good,” “[brand] complaints”), the model pulls from Reddit threads, local news, BBB profiles, and employee reviews. One viral incident at one franchise can become the first paragraph of every brand-level answer for a year.

There’s a second audience here that franchise brands tend to forget. Prospective franchisees ask AI tools the same questions customers do, plus harder ones: “is [brand] a good franchise to buy,” “[brand] franchisee lawsuits,” “[brand] franchise failure rate.” Your franchise development pipeline depends on those answers too.

Stop managing the average. Manage the bottom 10% of locations. That’s where the AI finds your worst sentences.

The operating model for franchise reputation management at scale

Here’s the structure that actually holds up across hundreds of locations. Each layer depends on the one before it.

1. Fix location data before anything else

AI assistants can’t recommend a location they can’t verify. Wrong hours, a disconnected phone number, or a duplicate profile makes a location look unreliable to both people and machines.

Audit every listing for name, address, phone, hours, categories, and attributes. Kill duplicates. Give every location its own page on your site with unique content and LocalBusiness schema that references the parent organization. A page that says “Tampa Westshore, open until 11 p.m., free parking in the rear lot” gives an AI something concrete to cite. A page that swaps the city name into a template doesn’t.

2. Chase review velocity, not review totals

A location with 1,400 reviews and nothing new since spring loses to a location with 300 reviews and 12 from last week. Both consumers and AI systems weigh recency.

Build review requests into the moment of service: the receipt, the post-appointment text, the QR code at checkout. Set a monthly floor per location based on transaction volume, and flag any location that misses it two months in a row.

Keep it clean. The FTC’s Consumer Review Rule bans fake reviews (including AI-written ones), buying reviews, and suppressing negative ones, and the agency sent a new round of warning letters to businesses in December 2025. Review gating, where you only ask happy customers, violates Google’s policies as well. A franchisee running a “five stars for a free smoothie” promo puts the whole brand at risk, not just their store.

3. Respond at scale without sounding like a template

Half of consumers penalize generic replies. Fifty identical “We’re sorry to hear about your experience, please contact us” responses across a brand’s profiles is exactly what that looks like.

A workable tiered setup:

  1. Headquarters writes the playbook: tone, what can be offered, what must be escalated.
  2. AI drafts the first response using the review’s actual details.
  3. A local manager edits and posts within 24 to 48 hours.
  4. Anything touching safety, discrimination, legal threats, or media goes to corporate within hours, not days.

The goal is a response that mentions the barista’s name, the specific wait time, or the fix you made. That’s what a reader believes, and it’s what gives an AI a positive, specific passage to pull from.

4. Write reputation into the franchise agreement

Most franchise reputation problems are governance problems in disguise.

Who owns the Google Business Profile: the franchisee or the brand? Who holds admin access? What’s the response SLA, and what happens when a franchisee ignores it? What happens to the profiles and their review history when a franchisee sells or exits?

A multi-unit operator who exits the system can walk away holding primary ownership on a dozen profiles, and getting those back through Google support can take months. Put ownership, access, response standards, and review solicitation rules in the operations manual, and tie them to the same compliance reviews you use for food safety or brand standards.

5. Monitor what AI actually says, by market

Rank tracking doesn’t cover this. You need a prompt set.

Build 20 to 40 prompts per priority market that mirror how people really ask: “best [category] near [neighborhood],” “[brand] [city] reviews,” “is [brand] worth it,” “[brand] complaints.” Run them monthly across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Mode, and Copilot. Log which locations appear, what’s said about them, and which sources get cited.

The citations are the useful part. They tell you whether a stale Yelp page, a 2024 local news story, or a Reddit thread is shaping the answer, and which location needs attention first.

The metrics that matter now

Notice that brand-wide average rating isn’t on the list. It belongs in the board deck, not in the operating review.

When one location goes sideways

It will happen. A viral video, a health inspection, an employee lawsuit. The first 48 hours decide whether it stays a local story or becomes the brand’s permanent AI summary.

  • Respond publicly and specifically on the affected profile within hours.
  • Publish a factual statement on the location page and brand newsroom, with dates, so there’s an accurate source to cite.
  • Brief every other location’s manager so they don’t improvise answers in their own reviews.
  • Watch brand-level AI prompts daily for two weeks and document which sources start getting cited.
  • Build credible, positive coverage after the fact. Suppressing one article does little if 30 forum threads quote it.

At NetReputation, franchise reputation management engagements usually start with the bottom decile of locations and a prompt audit in the brand’s top markets, because that’s where the gap between what headquarters believes and what AI says is widest.

The real shift

For years, enterprise reputation management meant protecting the brand name and letting locations handle their own reviews. That split doesn’t work anymore. AI assistants read the brand through its locations, one review stream at a time, and they recommend very few of them.

Every location is now a spokesperson. The brands that treat them that way will be the 1.2% that get named.

FAQ

What is franchise reputation management?

Franchise reputation management is the process of monitoring and improving how a franchise brand and each location are perceived online, including reviews, business listings, search results, and AI-generated answers. It requires coordination between the franchisor, which owns the brand, and franchisees, who run the operations that generate customer reviews.

How is enterprise reputation management different from managing one business?

Enterprise reputation management covers hundreds or thousands of locations at once, each with its own listings, reviews, and local search presence. It depends on centralized data management, response playbooks, governance over who controls each profile, and monitoring that tracks both brand-level and location-level perception across platforms and AI tools.

How do AI assistants choose which locations to recommend?

AI assistants are far more selective than Google’s local results. SOCi’s 2026 Local Visibility Index of 2,751 brands and about 350,000 locations found that ChatGPT recommended 1.2% of locations and Gemini 11%, compared with 35.9% visibility in Google’s local 3-pack. Recommended locations averaged 4.3 stars on ChatGPT and 4.2 on Perplexity, and accurate, consistent listing data also plays a role.

How many consumers use AI to find local businesses?

BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey found 45% of U.S. consumers use AI tools for local business recommendations, up from 6% in 2025. ChatGPT was the most used AI tool at 31% of AI users, followed by Google’s AI Mode at 23%. Most AI users still verify recommendations by checking reviews on the original platform.

How fast should franchise locations respond to reviews?

Aim for under 48 hours, and faster for serious complaints. BrightLocal’s 2026 survey found 19% of consumers expect a same-day response and 81% expect one within a week. Half of consumers are unlikely to choose a business that posts generic, templated replies, so responses should reference specific details from the review.

Can a franchisor be affected by a franchisee’s review practices?

Yes. Fake reviews, paid reviews, incentives tied to positive ratings, and review gating violate the FTC’s Consumer Review Rule and Google’s policies. A single franchisee’s violation can trigger profile penalties, regulatory attention, and negative press that attaches to the whole brand, which is why review rules belong in the franchise operations manual.

The software leverages reinforcement learning models to parse unstructured financial news, real-time order books, social sentiment vectors, and historical macroeconomic data simultaneously. By plugging securely via cryptographic API keys into a user’s existing brokerage and digital asset exchange accounts, the agents design, backtest, and execute complex, long-horizon trading strategies, dynamically adjusting position sizing, hedging risks, and managing stop-loss structures under human-set risk parameters.

content.rendered:
PsiQuantum, a Palo Alto, CA-based builder of quantum computers, received a conditional commitment for a loan of up to $150m from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC).

The loan will expand the company’s advanced manufacturing and prototyping capabilities in the United States. The financing would support PsiQuantum’s 140,000-square-foot hub in Milpitas, California, for scaling the company’s technologies and developing and validating the prototype systems that underpin its fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture.   • Test equipment for the fabrication and validation of components, subassemblies, and system-level assemblies
  • Critical infrastructure for system assembly, integration, and testing
  • Advanced cryogenic systems for prototype systems

Led by Victor Peng, Chief Executive Officer, PsiQuantum aims to build and deploy useful quantum computers via a photonic approach that enables it to leverage high-volume semiconductor manufacturing, existing cryogenic infrastructure, and architectural flexibility to rapidly scale its systems.

PsiQuantum’s potential financing from the Department of War would be deployed by the company to expand and strengthen domestic quantum computing capacity.

In July 2026, the company announced a new $125m expanded agreement with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) under DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. PsiQuantum has partnered with DARPA under this evaluation program since 2022. Since 2022, PsiQuantum has worked closely with the Air Force Research Lab to advance semiconductor chip manufacturing and silicon photonics expertise for the U.S. Air Force.

title.rendered: OllyGarden Raises $4M in Funding

content.rendered:
OllyGarden, a Berlin, Germany-based provider of a platform fixing bad telemetry to give observability engineers data they can use, raised $4m in funding. 

Backers included Next Frontier Capital, Grand Ventures, ACTAI, and DIG Ventures.

Launched in 2025 by Juraci Paixão Kröhling, OllyGarden provides companies across retail, financial services and enterprise software with a platform that continuously evaluates telemetry quality, identifies issues, and then turns findings into source-level fixes. This enables engineers and AI agents to make decisions based on clear data and stop bad information from seeping into wider operations. 

In addition to the new capital, OllyGarden is today also announcing the launch of its latest product innovation: Minimum Viable Instrumentation (MVI). title.rendered: Why Coalition Loyalty Is Moving Beyond Airlines, Hotels, and Credit Cards

content.rendered:
For the longest time, customer loyalty was a one-brand deal. When it came to a particular type of purchase, such as coffee or flights, you typically stuck with one company and earned rewards for coming back.

Coalition loyalty took that idea, ran with it, and opened it up. One loyalty program could now involve several businesses, giving members more ways to earn rewards and potentially more places to redeem them. Some networks even let customers carry a shared membership status across participating brands.

Airlines are one of the earliest and most familiar examples of coalition loyalty. What were once simple frequent-flyer programs now extend well beyond flights, looping in retailers, credit cards, hotels, and other relevant businesses into one expansive rewards network. Other businesses, like retailers and digital entertainment companies, have since started adopting the model, exploring loyalty programs that let customers earn and use rewards across several brands.

Why Put Loyalty Into a Shared Network?

There’s plenty of appeal with a standalone loyalty program—customers are encouraged to choose you, and businesses get a direct way to reward their own customers. The problem is that there’s a natural limit to how often those customers can use it, as there are only so many opportunities to earn or use those rewards depending on how often they interact with that business.

When brands participate in a multi-brand network, customers get more places to earn and use rewards, while participating businesses can benefit from being connected to other brands. Depending on how the network is structured, that can mean:

  • Increased usefulness of the membership as customers can use it across different parts of everyday spending
  • More reason for customers to stay active, with more occasions to interact with the program
  • Greater exposure to customers who already use other participating brands
  • More cross-selling opportunities
  • Shared cost of loyalty infrastructure rather than building everything independently
  • Stronger incentive for partners to participate
  • Less competition with other standalone points programs
  • Potential generation of insights into customer behavior data

Although these benefits exist, they will likely vary from one coalition to another given the differences in programs. Overall, though, a broader network increases relevancy outside of any single purchase or brand. There’s also a reinforcing effect for the businesses involved since the larger customer base can make the network more appealing to potential partners, and a useful rewards network gives customers more reason to sign up. At the same time, adding more partners can also make a program harder to understand if rates and rules vary too much across the network.

Coalition Loyalty Beyond Traditional Industries

While retailers and airlines may be the easiest places to spot multi-brand loyalty, the model isn’t tied to any of them. Digital businesses can also form coalitions, particularly when several related brands want customers to maintain one loyalty relationship across their services. Being part of a coalition can be a useful choice when customers already move between those brands in the same category, since they don’t necessarily need a separate account, status system, or points balance for each one.

That setup can also change what the loyalty program is doing. Rather than reward repeat purchases from one company, the network gives customers a reason to stay within a group of connected businesses. Online entertainment is a great example of how this can work. CanadaCasino’s look at loyalty networks examines Casino Rewards, a shared program in which one membership works across multiple casino brands. Members can earn loyalty points across the network and carry their VIP status across participating brands.

The important part isn’t the type of business involved but the architecture behind the program. Customers stick to one membership that connects them to multiple brands, while the businesses share the infrastructure needed to manage rewards and member activity across the network.

How the Loyalty Network Works Underneath

On the customer’s side, a shared loyalty program is made to appear glaringly simple. Customers are presented with an account, a points balance, and a way to earn and redeem rewards. The technical setup behind the interface has a system that must keep track of much more. At the most basic level, it needs to recognize the same member across different participating brands and keep their account activity up to date. Then it needs to handle different redemption and earning rules, manage different membership statuses or tiers, and track points as they move through the network. Some programs will even offer more personalization and customer data permissions to manage, increasing complexity.

On top of these moving parts, there’s the financial side that gets more complicated as more brands join the network. If one company issues the points and another accepts them for redemption, the system should record those transactions and record the value moving between participating businesses. Of course, the customer doesn’t need to see what’s happening behind the scenes, which is why all of this appears as a single points balance. Look deeper, though, and coalition loyalty is much more of a technology and infrastructure problem than just another marketing campaign.

When More Partners Add Real Value

A loyalty network doesn’t just become more valuable as more brands get added to it. Each new partner needs to bring something useful to the relationship for customers and for the businesses already involved. Customers might enjoy less loyalty fragmentation and gain more relevant rewards. Businesses, meanwhile, need a reason to join and stay, whether that means reaching new customers or accessing infrastructure they would otherwise have to build themselves. 

When customers interact with multiple businesses through the same membership, the network can also provide a broader view of their purchasing behavior and engagement across those brands. While that information can be useful, it raises new questions. For example, what information can each partner access? What has the customer agreed to share? Who controls the data in the ecosystem, how is it protected, and to what degree? When a business leaves the network, what happens to all the customer information?

Since digital privacy and data governance are being treated more and more seriously, these issues need to be considered alongside the technology used once the coalition program begins.

When More Partners Add Real Value

The strength of a coalition is primarily about how well brand relationships work together. And while that concept is simple, making it work is much more complicated. Behind a shared membership often sits a web of business relationships and rules that customers rarely see. As loyalty networks move into more industries, the infrastructure supporting them will likely become just as important as the customer rewards. Could the next generation of loyalty be less about the rewards themselves and more about the infrastructure that lets them move more freely between brands?

title.rendered: $10 Million and Counting: Hola Prime Hits Major Trader Payout Milestone

content.rendered:
New York, USA, October 6th, 2026, FinanceWire

Hola Prime, the global proprietary trading firm known for its 1-Hour Payout model, today announced it has paid out more than $10 million to its funded traders. The milestone caps a period of rapid growth for the firm, which has built its reputation on speed, transparency and consistency in how traders get paid.

Across the $10 million distributed, the average payout to a Hola Prime trader stands at approximately $1,800. The firm’s fastest payout to date was processed in 36 seconds from request to completion, and its highest total payout to a single trader reached $70,776.

“Crossing $10 million isn’t a number we’re celebrating for its own sake. Every dollar of it is a trader who followed the rules, managed their risk and got paid on time.,” said Somesh Kapuria, CEO of Hola Prime. “When we launched the 1-Hour Payout, a lot of people in this industry said it couldn’t be done at scale. Ten million dollars later, the data speaks for itself. Our commitment is simple: if you earn it, you get it, and you get it fast.”

Hola Prime’s approach has earned it industry recognition, including Global Most Transparent Prop Firm from Finance Magnates and Fastest Payout Prop Firm MEA at the UF Awards. The firm holds a 4.5 rating on Trustpilot from more than 3,000 reviews.

The $10 million milestone was reached under Hola Prime’s 1 Hour Payout commitment, which measures payout processing from the moment a trader submits a withdrawal request to the release of funds. While many prop firms begin measuring processing time only after a withdrawal has been approved, Hola Prime starts the clock at the point of submission, setting a higher standard for payout speed and accountability. The firm also publishes payout data and challenge pass rates, while its Prime Circle programme gives traders who complete five successful payouts an additional 5% on every subsequent payout.

“Ten million is a milestone, not a finish line,” Somesh Kapuria added. “Our next target is to get there again in a fraction of the time, and to keep proving that a prop firm can be fast, transparent and fair all at once.”

About Hola Prime

Hola Prime is a global prop trading firm offering funded trading accounts to skilled traders worldwide. Known for its 1-Hour Payout model, Hola Prime provides traders with access to significant capital across major financial instruments including Forex, commodities and indices. With a rapidly growing trader base, Hola Prime continues to redefine expectations in prop trading.

For more information visit www.holaprime.com

title.rendered: STARCARES Equips Seven Foster Homes for Children and Young People in Tanzania

content.rendered:
Moshi, Tanzania, October 5th, 2026, FinanceWire

The initiative with Kijana Kwanza furnishes seven family-style homes for up to 250 beneficiaries in Tanzania.

STARCARES, the CSR initiative of STARTRADER, has partnered with Kijana Kwanza in Tanzania to equip seven new foster homes for up to 250 beneficiaries. By turning newly built housing into safe, functional homes, the initiative supports the stability children need to continue their education and move towards greater independence.

STARCARES has provided beds, mattresses, bedding, wardrobes, cooking stoves, dining tables and chairs, enabling the homes to function from day one. The support forms part of its Where Tomorrow STARs Begin programme, focused on education, youth development and long-term opportunity.

Kijana Kwanza, meaning “Young People First,” is a Moshi-based NGO providing holistic care for 250 beneficiaries aged 5–22 through education, vocational training, life skills, shelter and community programmes, with its wider programme of services reaching over 23,000 people

“STARCARES is helping us turn these new houses into real homes. Their support provides the everyday essentials our children need to live with dignity, stability and care from the moment they move in.” — Mujibu Idrisa Abeid, CEO, Kijana Kwanza 

For many of the children supported by Kijana Kwanza, a secure home is the foundation for staying in education, building practical skills, growing in confidence and progressing towards independence.

“What matters most is giving young people the stability to feel safe today and the confidence to imagine a different tomorrow. That is the value we want STARCARES to create: support that strengthens lives and opens opportunities for the future.”— Muhammed Padhani, CCO of STARTRADER

The Tanzania initiative builds on STARCARES’ work in Nigeria, Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines, reaching more communities where young people need safer spaces, greater care and stronger opportunities.

Guided by its principle, “Bringing STAR, Delivering CARE,” STARCARES continues expanding its reach where support is needed most, turning essential needs into stronger foundations for young people to live, learn and move forward with confidence.

About STARTRADER

STARTRADER is a global multi-asset broker empowering retail and institutional partners to access global markets through a range of platforms, including MetaTrader, STARTRADER APP, and STAR Copy.

STARTRADER operates through entities licensed and regulated by authorities including CMA, ASIC, FSCA, FSA and FSC, combining strong governance with a client-first approach, serving both retail clients and partners with a commitment to transparency, reliability, and long-term growth.

title.rendered: Tryp.com Raises USD1.9M in Seed Funding

content.rendered:
Tryp.com, a Copenhagen, Denmark-based travel technology and multi-modal booking platform, raised USD1.9m in seed funding.

The round, which brought total funding to USD5.9m, was led by Point Capital Partners, with participation from returning early-stage investor Iberis Capital alongside a strategic syndicate of travel industry angel investors.

The company will use the capital fo its international market entry into Asia and the Americas, engineering development of its real-time itinerary-building engine, the launch of automated tours and leisure experience booking features, and for the scale of its business-to-business (B2B) enterprise partnerships with global commercial airlines.

Tryp.com develops an advanced multi-modal travel orchestration platform and AI-driven curation engine engineered to automate complex multi-stop trip planning. The cloud-native system operates by ingesting a user’s baseline budget and travel windows. Its algorithmic routing engine continuously tracks and maps over 80 million real-time transit fares spanning global flights, trains, buses, and ferries, alongside 28 million accommodation listings, automatically combining them into single-click multi-city itineraries.

The platform features a context-aware “For You” discovery feed and a 24/7 AI travel companion named Sandra.

Serving over 10m lifetime users, the core booking engine also operates as the primary enterprise software infrastructure powering WIZZ Holidays, the official holiday and package platform for European low-cost carrier Wizz Air.

title.rendered: How Small Business Owners Can Create Social Media Images with an AI Image Generator

content.rendered:
Small businesses often need fresh images for product launches, promotions, and seasonal posts. But creating every visual through a new photo shoot can be expensive and time-consuming.

Pollo AI’s AI image generator gives sellers another way to create social media visuals from a written idea or an existing product image. The best approach depends on what the post needs to show. A product image, a lifestyle scene, and a promotional graphic should be planned differently.

Start by Choosing the Type of Image

Before using the AI image generator from Pollo AI, the seller should decide what the image is for.

A product post should keep the item clear and easy to recognize. A simple background usually works best for new arrivals or product highlights.

A lifestyle image can show the product in use or in a setting that fits the target customer. For example, a reusable bottle could appear on a hiking trail, while a candle could be placed in a relaxed home setting.

Promotional posts need room for a headline, discount, or date. The seller should plan this space before generating the image.

The format matters too. Square images work well for many feed posts, vertical images suit mobile-first content, and wide images are useful for banners or cover visuals.

How to Create Social Media Images with Pollo AI’s AI Image Generator

1. Pick a Style That Fits the Post

Pollo AI offers multiple image-generation models in one workspace. The seller can try different models when the first result does not fit the campaign. For social media campaigns that also require short video content, the DeepAI video generator can be explored alongside image-generation tools within Pollo AI. 

Realistic images often work well for food, beauty products, furniture, and other items where texture matters. Illustrated or stylized visuals may be a better fit for holiday campaigns, service promotions, or educational posts.

The seller should choose a style that supports the brand rather than simply selecting the most dramatic result.

2. Describe One Clear Scene

The prompt should make the main subject obvious.

For example, a coffee shop could write:

“A cold brew coffee in a clear glass on a small wooden café table, soft morning sunlight, realistic photography, relaxed atmosphere, vertical social media format.”

This gives the image generator a clear product, setting, and mood.

Trying to include several products, locations, and visual effects in one prompt can make the image look busy. It is usually better to start with one simple scene and add details only when needed.

3. Use a Real Product Image for Important Details

Text prompts can create new concepts, but they may not reproduce a specific product accurately.

If the seller already has a good product photo, it can be used as a reference when the product has distinctive packaging, branding, or design details.

For example, a skincare brand could use a real bottle image and create a new bathroom or stone background around it. This can produce a fresh campaign image while keeping the product closer to its actual appearance.

The final image should still be checked carefully. Labels, edges, colors, and small details may change during generation.

4. Generate a Few Options and Compare Them

The first result is not always the best one. If the product looks right but the setting feels wrong, the seller can change only the background or lighting and generate another version.

For example, changing “bright modern kitchen” to “warm home kitchen with soft evening light” may be enough to shift the mood.

The seller should compare a few versions and choose the one that communicates the message most clearly. The most detailed image is not always the most useful for social media.

5. Add Text After the Image Is Ready

Product names, prices, dates, and calls to action are usually easier to control in a separate design tool. AI-generated text can contain spelling mistakes or uneven lettering.

The seller should also preview the finished post on a phone. Small text and detailed backgrounds may be difficult to see in a mobile feed.

Keep the Post Clear and Accurate

A social media image should communicate one main idea. A product post should make the item easy to recognize, while a seasonal campaign can use relevant colors or settings. Service businesses may focus on a clear result, such as a clean room for a cleaning company or a well-groomed pet for a grooming service.

Before publishing, the seller should check that the product’s color, shape, labels, and key details are accurate. The image should not show features or results the business cannot provide.

The final post should also be reviewed at its intended size. If the product looks too small, the text is hard to read, or the layout feels crowded on a phone, a simpler version may work better.

Conclusion

Pollo AI’s AI image generator can help small businesses create product posts, lifestyle visuals, and promotional content without arranging a new photo shoot for every campaign.

The process is straightforward: choose the type of image, build one clear scene, use a real product reference when accuracy matters, and review the final result before publishing. title.rendered: Rig Security, Interview With CEO Guy Kozliner

content.rendered:
Rig Security, a Tel Aviv, Israel-based provider of an identity protection platform, emerged from stealth raising $12M in seed funding. In conjunction with the funding announcement, CEO Guy Kozliner replied to our questions about the company, the product, the funding and future plans.

FinSMEs: Hi Guy, can you tell us a bit more about yourself? What’s your background?

I’m the Founder and CEO of Rig Security. Before starting Rig, I worked for the CTO team at Wiz, and previously held engineering and operational roles at Cybereason. I also served in the Israeli Intelligence Corps.

At Wiz, I saw the value of context across assets and environments so teams could understand how issues create broader risks. That perspective strongly influenced the DNA of my vision. We’re applying it to identity: understanding how people, non-human identities, and AI agents are connected, what they can access, the cross-platform trusted relationship and how to protect that access in runtime.

FinSMEs: Let’s speak about Rig Security. What is the market problem you want to solve? What is the real opportunity?

Enterprises have spent decades deciding which people should have access to which systems. AI introduces another question: which agents are using that access right now, and what are they doing with it? The focus is shifting from who can access what to what trusted access enables agents to do.

AI agents operate through the credentials and sessions of the employee or service account that launched them. In a security log, an agent taking a dangerous action can look exactly like the person whose account it’s using. That makes it difficult to identify the actual actor and intervene precisely.

Rig connects that activity to a unified view of identities, permissions, and trust relationships across the organization. We help security teams understand the exposure, distinguish agent activity from human activity, and enforce controls while agents operate.

The opportunity is to give enterprises the confidence to adopt AI more broadly while maintaining control over the access it uses.

FinSMEs: What are the features differentiating the product from competitors?

Two capabilities are central to our differentiation: correlating identities across systems and controlling identity activity at runtime.

Our proprietary Rig Identity Correlation Engine, or RICE, identifies the same identity across different environments with more than 96% accuracy. It powers a live graph showing how human, non-human, and AI identities connect through accounts, permissions, sessions, and trust relationships. That context helps teams identify dangerous access paths that are difficult to see when each system is examined separately.

Our lightweight endpoint agent then shows what is happening on the device, including local credentials and identities that legacy solutions usually miss. It distinguishes an AI agent’s session from the user’s own activity and can block a risky agent action before it reaches the cloud, without interrupting the person’s work.

Together, these capabilities bring identity posture management, threat detection, and response into one platform. Organizations can connect agentlessly in minutes and add endpoint sensors for runtime attribution and enforcement.

FinSMEs: You just raised a new funding round. Please, tell us more about it.

We’re announcing $12 million in seed funding, co-led by Ten Eleven Ventures and Brightmind Partners, with strategic participation from CrowdStrike and backing from many cybersecurity founders and executives, including Wiz co-founder and CTO, Ami Luttwak.

That brings together experience across identity, endpoint, and cloud security- the areas that need to work together to address this problem.

The round supports our next stage as we emerge from stealth, building on a platform that is already operating in enterprise production environments, including Fortune 200.

FinSMEs: Can you share some numbers and achievements for the business?

We’re already in production with Fortune 200 organizations, with deployments across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and technology. Rig analyzes and protects hundreds of millions of identity events and access signals each month, and our team has grown to 20 people.

We’re also available through the AWS Marketplace and CrowdStrike Marketplace. Another milestone was finishing among the top three startups in the 2025 AWS and CrowdStrike Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator, held in collaboration with NVIDIA’s Inception program.

What matters most to us is that customers are using Rig in production to address a problem they’re encountering today: understanding which agents are operating, whose access those agents are using, and how to control their actions without getting in employees’ way.

FinSMEs: What are your medium-term plans?
Our focus is to deepen the platform and expand adoption among enterprises as AI agents become part of everyday work.

On the product side, that means extending visibility into agent activity, strengthening runtime controls, and making it easier for security teams to resolve identity risks safely. We also want to build on our enterprise deployments and marketplace presence to reach more organizations.

The principle guiding us is straightforward: security should help businesses move forward confidently. As more work is delegated to AI, organizations need to know what those agents can access and have the ability to intervene when necessary. That’s the foundation we’re building.

title.rendered: STARTRADER Raises Lloyd’s of London Client Fund Insurance to USD 30 Million in Aggregate

content.rendered:
Port Louis, Mauritius, September 29th, 2026, FinanceWire

The aggregate cover increases thirtyfold from USD 1 million, applies to available balances and open positions in the event of insolvency, and remains free to clients.

Startrader Financial Markets Limited (Mauritius) has raised the aggregate limit of its client fund insurance, underwritten by Arch and other Lloyd’s of London syndicates, from USD 1 million to USD 30 million, effective October 1, 2026. The policy covers available balances and collateral supporting open positions, responding above a per-client retention where insolvency coincides with covered misconduct.

Client fund protection increasingly shapes broker choice. Because insolvency is remote, cover size often goes unexamined until it matters, making early action a governance decision, not a marketing one.

The policy covers only eligible clients of this entity, not other STARTRADER entities, and complements its segregation of client funds from company assets.

“Insurance is not something clients think about on a good day. It matters on the worst one, and a ceiling that only looks adequate until it is tested is not much of a ceiling.” – Peter Karsten, CEO, STARTRADER.

The higher limit will apply automatically from October 1, 2026, with no action required. Claims must be submitted to the appointed insolvency practitioner, with an Investor Compensation Claim Form, within 12 months of the insolvency event.

About STARTRADER

STARTRADER is a global multi-asset broker empowering retail and institutional partners to access global markets through a range of platforms, including MetaTrader, STARTRADER APP, and STAR Copy. Regulated in five jurisdictions (CMA, ASIC, FSCA, FSA, and FSC), STARTRADER combines strong governance with a client-first approach, serving both retail clients and partners with a commitment to transparency, reliability, and long-term growth.

Disclaimer: This announcement is for information only and is not investment advice or tailored to your circumstances. Forward-looking statements cannot be guaranteed. The insurance is an excess-of-loss policy subject to its full terms, conditions and exclusions, which prevail in any conflict. It covers only loss of client cash or securities caused by covered misconduct following an insolvency event, not trading losses. Payments may be less than a client’s loss and depend on the insolvency practitioner’s determinations and the firm’s policy compliance. Clients are beneficiaries of a discretionary trust with no direct claim against the insurer. CFDs are high risk and may not suit all investors. Not intended for distribution where contrary to local law or regulation.
