title.rendered: One Biosciences Receives €3.3M in Non-Dilutive Public Funding

content.rendered:
One Biosciences, a Paris, France-based techbio and single-cell precision oncology startup, received €3.3m in non-dilutive public funding.

The grant was awarded by Bpifrance under the i-Démo 5 project call, an integral part of the government’s France 2030 nationwide industrial and innovation investment initiative.

The funding will finance the CAST (Cancer Single-cell Analysis for Therapy) project, a four-year clinical translation program executed in direct commercial and medical collaboration with Institut Curie, France’s leading oncological research center and specialized hospital group.

The company will use the funds to industrialize its proprietary molecular profiling platform, validate predictive biomarkers for aggressive oncology variants, prepare for CE-IVD international regulatory approvals, and scale its centralized clinical laboratory infrastructure within the Paris region ahead of commercial deployment.

Spun off in 2020 from Institut Curie, One Biosciences addresses a critical diagnostic blind spot in the treatment of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC), which accounts for 15% to 20% of all breast cancer cases.

The company develops OneMap™, an end-to-end single-cell transcriptomics and artificial intelligence platform designed to function as an in vitro diagnostic tool to guide personalized oncology treatment paths. The system processes standard hospital tumor tissue biopsies, running high-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing to analyze cellular structures at the resolution of individual cells. By deploying specialized machine learning algorithms to isolate specific cell sub-populations driving resistance, the software generates fully auditable, clinically actionable predictive reports within a two-week turnaround time.

Led by Chief Executive Officer Hedi Ben Brahim alongside co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer Dr. Céline Vallot, the CAST program will leverage a clinical cohort of over 300 TNBC patients across Institut Curie’s Institute of Women’s Cancers to compile a large annotated single-cell dataset for triple-negative breast cancer, enabling doctors to safely de-escalate treatments for positive responders or precisely pivot salvage therapies for high-risk patients.

Buenos Aires, Argentina, September 28th, 2026, FinanceWire

PU Prime strengthened its engagement with Argentina’s financial sector through its participation in FX Expo Buenos Aires 2026, held on September 17–18 at Golden Center Eventos. The event brought together investors, industry professionals, and market enthusiasts from across Latin America, providing PU Prime with a medium to connect with local traders. As an Official Regional Sponsor of AFA, PU Prime used the expo to demonstrate how its football partnership translates into engagement opportunities beyond traditional brand sponsorship. Mr. Cohen discussed the strategic considerations behind the partnership and how collaboration is helping PU Prime establish deeper connections with local communities, particularly within the rapidly evolving Latin American market. During a panel interview, Mr. Cohen expressed his opinion that online trading is transforming financial markets by expanding digital access to global opportunities while increasing the need for financial education and risk awareness. In this evolving environment, he believed that PU Prime played an important role in connecting global financial opportunities with the specific needs and characteristics of individual markets.

Moving forward, our goal is to build on this foundation by continuously refining our services and deepening our engagement with the local trading community,” said Mr. Cohen during his speech at FX Expo Buenos Aires 2026.

title.rendered: CEO FinteqHub: Banks Need to Conduct Thousands of Testing Cycles Before Granting AI Full Access to Payments

content.rendered:
The mass adoption of AI agents will not replace marketplace infrastructure. Instead, these assistants are more likely to become part of it. This will reshape user behavior and shopping journeys, but e-commerce platforms will remain at the center of online retail.

AI Agents vs. Traditional Online Shopping

The development of AI agents will not eliminate traditional online shopping. Instead, it will split shopping into two parallel scenarios, with consumers retaining the choice of which one to use.

People will increasingly delegate routine and rational purchases — those where the desired outcome is clear in advance — to AI agents. Instead of spending half an hour comparing dozens of product listings, a user will simply formulate a request: “Find a white T-shirt with good reviews for under €30” — and the agent will analyze the price, seller rating, and reviews within seconds and return with a ready-made solution.

However, there are certain purchases that people are unlikely to ever fully delegate to AI, because users enjoy making choices themselves. This includes browsing a new clothing collection, comparing interior design items, or searching for the one product that immediately catches their attention. In such cases, purchasing decisions are driven not only by rational logic, but also by emotion.

A large share of users visit marketplaces not to make a specific purchase, but simply to relax and browse products. For many people, visiting e-commerce platforms has become as habitual as scrolling through social media, and not everyone will want to give up the familiar experience of manually browsing online storefronts.

As Vadim Drozd, CEO of payment infrastructure company FinteqHub, notes: ”Although Europe’s banking infrastructure is becoming ready for agentic commerce, consumers should understand that the current stage of AI agent development still resembles an open alpha test, with much of the risk from erroneous actions ultimately falling on the user.”

An AI agent needs to consider many parameters before making a purchase. “Price is only one of them”, as highlighted by Drozd. “When buying an airline ticket, for example, the agent must take into account departure and arrival times, the number of connections, baggage allowance, refund and ticket-change conditions. The program may formally complete the task and purchase a ticket for the correct date, staying within a set budget, while still selecting a non-refundable fare or an option without checked baggage. From the payment system’s perspective, such a transaction may be fully valid and authorized even though the outcome does not meet the user’s expectations. In some cases, it may also be impossible to cancel or refund a ticket purchased under those conditions.”

AI agents can handle the rational side of consumer demand, but they cannot replace its emotional component. You cannot ask an assistant to want something on the user’s behalf — which means browsing product feeds in search of something that suddenly sparks interest will remain a human prerogative.

At the same time, delegating routine purchases to an agent changes the mechanics of selling itself. An AI agent cannot be attracted by a bright banner, a sale label, or an “only one item left” trigger. It is not susceptible to manipulation and instead compares objective parameters such as price, product characteristics, and customer reviews. The winner will no longer be the seller shouting the loudest through advertising banners, but the one whose metrics are objectively better. This opens the door to new advertising tools designed not for humans, but for AI agents acting as analytical shopping assistants.

Marketplaces Are Sellers’ Allies, Not Their Enemies

Another popular argument is that AI agents will learn to find products directly from manufacturers, cutting marketplaces and their commissions out of the chain. However, this claim overlooks one of the core functions of marketplaces: these platforms do not exist simply to collect intermediary fees. They provide a ready-made commercial environment that is extremely expensive to build from scratch and is not always efficient for individual sellers to maintain themselves.

Direct sales require entrepreneurs to become deeply involved in processes outside their core business. Manufacturers have to independently maintain websites and accounting systems, communicate with customers, process payments, build logistics networks, and handle returns. Add recurring investment in customer acquisition and marketing, and maintaining an independent e-commerce operation becomes economically impractical for most businesses.

It is also important to recognize that an AI agent simply cannot replace every business process. In addition to digital services, e-commerce includes “real-world” operations that require physical infrastructure — warehousing, logistics, packaging, and more.

Moreover, an AI agent will decide where it is more cost-effective and reliable to purchase a product. To do so, it will analyze not only price, but also seller ratings, reviews, delivery speed and cost, return policies, and other parameters. Small independent online stores may simply lack some of this data, while the scale and quality of the information they provide may be inferior to the datasets accumulated by major marketplaces.

Advertising Tools Will Transform

Changes in online retail will inevitably affect traditional advertising mechanisms. AI agents do not interact with conventional advertising banners, but this does not signal a crisis in promotion. Rather, it marks a new stage in the evolution of advertising tools.

Traditional internet search is already at the forefront of this transformation. Search is becoming increasingly agent-driven, and this shift is happening much faster and on a significantly larger scale than the transformation of the advertising market. However, this paradigm shift does not mean the decline of search engines. Google remains at the forefront of the industry developing search agents: the company invests more heavily in these technologies than anyone else, retains the largest market share, and achieves the strongest results.

E-commerce is likely to follow the same path. The emergence of agentic commerce is creating entirely new marketing tools designed to work with product selection and ranking algorithms. As AI assistants become widely adopted, marketplaces themselves will begin actively introducing and adapting these solutions within their own ecosystems.

Visual advertising cues will increasingly be replaced by algorithmic prioritization, allowing products to come to the attention of AI assistants. As a result, sellers will gain more precise and flexible promotional tools, while platforms will gain additional opportunities to expand their monetization capabilities and develop new technology partnerships.

Moreover, in this model, AI assistants need marketplaces just as much as consumers do. To select a product and place an order, an agent must understand not only what the user wants, but also how they prefer to receive the purchase — for example, through next-day delivery or pickup from the nearest collection point. This requires a broad assortment and up-to-date data on products, prices, availability, and delivery. Marketplaces already provide exactly this combination of information and infrastructure.

Why Marketplaces Will Build the Best Shopping Agents

Data is at the core of any effective recommendation algorithm. For an AI assistant to make genuinely accurate and useful purchasing decisions, it needs access to large-scale commercial analytics.

Today, the overwhelming majority of online transactions take place on marketplaces. By processing billions of orders across virtually every product category, these platforms accumulate unique large-scale datasets reflecting real consumer behavior.

There is a well-known principle in optimization: a universal algorithm designed to perform equally well across a wide range of tasks will lose to a highly specialized solution. The broader its scope, the lower its peak performance in individual tasks. Conversely, being the best in a specific domain requires sacrificing some degree of universality.

Shopping on a marketplace is a highly specialized task. To perform it well, a system must understand what people actually buy and how demand behaves in a specific category during a specific season.

External AI agents, no matter how sophisticated they may be, lack these capabilities. They can reason about products in general terms, analyze reviews, and formulate hypotheses, but this information alone will not be sufficient to compete with major e-commerce players.

What Will Actually Change

Marketplaces have already gone through the previous wave of AI adoption with the arrival of chatbots and generative AI models. Instead of competing with these technologies, they integrated them into their services. Today, AI helps consumers choose products, assists sellers in analyzing sales, and helps create product descriptions and visual content for listings.

As AI agents become widely adopted, rational and predictable purchases will increasingly be delegated to virtual assistants. However, the actual orders will continue to be placed through marketplaces, because price, delivery speed, and convenience — advantages that major platforms already know how to scale effectively — will remain among the most important factors.

Still, according to FinteqHub’s Vadim Drozd, banks and payment companies will have to solve numerous challenges. He said: 

“It is therefore not enough simply to set a spending limit and authorize an AI agent to make a payment. Consumers will need to define acceptable purchase conditions in advance, including the maximum price, permitted categories of goods and services, refund rules, acceptable additional charges, and the circumstances in which the agent must request further confirmation before completing a transaction. That said, banks need to conduct thousands of testing cycles before granting AI full access to payments.”

There is little doubt that AI agents will change the way consumers interact with online retail, with the conversational interface of an intelligent assistant increasingly becoming the gateway to shopping. However, behind every virtual agent there must be real-world infrastructure capable of packaging an order, dispatching it to the customer, and delivering it on time.

It is precisely this symbiosis that will define the next major stage in the evolution of e-commerce

title.rendered: Don’t Let One Forgotten Document Put Your Business at Risk, 9 Ways to Protect Confidential Information

content.rendered:
When people think about protecting confidential business information, their minds often go straight to cybersecurity, complicated passwords, suspicious emails, and hackers trying to break into company networks.

Those threats certainly deserve attention, but sensitive information can also be exposed in much simpler ways, including through an employee file left on a desk, a financial report forgotten beside a printer, or an old customer document placed in an ordinary recycling bin.

These situations can seem harmless because they are part of everyday office life, yet they can create unnecessary risks when the information involved includes personal details, financial data, contracts, employee records, medical information, or internal company documents. A business may spend heavily on digital security while overlooking the fact that confidential information still moves through filing cabinets, meeting rooms, printers, home offices, storage areas, and discarded equipment.

Protecting sensitive information therefore requires more than locking down computers. It means paying attention to how information is created, used, shared, stored, and eventually disposed of throughout its entire lifecycle. The good news is that businesses do not always need complicated systems to make meaningful improvements, because many of the strongest protections begin with clear policies, consistent habits, and employees who understand what is expected of them.

Here are nine practical ways businesses can strengthen those habits and reduce the chances of confidential information ending up where it should not.

1. Know Which Information Needs Extra Protection

Before a business can protect confidential information effectively, employees need to understand which information actually requires special care. Many organizations handle a mixture of public information, everyday internal documents, customer details, financial records, personnel files, contracts, passwords, health related information, and strategic business material, yet employees may not always know which categories carry the greatest risk.

A simple information classification system can make these decisions much easier. For example, a company might divide its information into categories such as public, internal, confidential, and highly restricted, with clear examples showing how each type should be handled. Employees then have practical guidance when deciding whether a document can remain on a shared desk, whether it belongs in locked storage, or whether access should be limited to specific people.

The system does not need to be complicated to be useful. In fact, overly complex rules can sometimes make employees less likely to follow them, especially when they are busy and simply trying to complete their work. Clear definitions and realistic examples are usually more effective because they allow people to recognize sensitive information quickly and make better decisions without constantly checking a policy manual.

2. Create a Clear Document Retention Policy

Keeping every business document forever may feel like the safest option, but retaining unnecessary information can actually increase the amount of sensitive material that needs to be protected. When filing cabinets, storage rooms, shared drives, and archives become crowded with outdated records, it becomes harder to know what still has value and what is simply creating additional exposure.

A document retention policy gives employees clear guidance about how long different types of records should be kept and what should happen once that period ends. Certain documents may need to be retained because of tax requirements, legal obligations, industry regulations, contractual commitments, or operational needs, while other records may no longer serve a useful purpose after a particular period.

Regularly reviewing stored information also makes day to day records management easier. Instead of allowing years of paperwork and digital files to accumulate without a plan, businesses can create predictable schedules for reviewing, archiving, and securely disposing of information. This approach reduces clutter while also limiting the volume of confidential material that could potentially be lost, misplaced, or accessed unnecessarily.

3. Control Who Can Access Sensitive Records

One of the simplest ways to reduce information security risks is to limit access to people who genuinely need the information to perform their jobs. When every employee can view every file or enter every storage area, confidential information is exposed to more people than necessary, even when nobody has harmful intentions.

For physical documents, access controls may involve locked filing cabinets, restricted records rooms, controlled keys, or procedures for checking sensitive files in and out. For digital records, similar principles can be applied through password protection, user permissions, secure folders, and role based access that gives employees only the information required for their responsibilities.

Access should also be reviewed whenever an employee changes positions, moves to another department, or leaves the organization. Permissions that made sense in a previous role may no longer be appropriate months later, yet outdated access is easy to overlook when there is no regular review process. By making access reviews part of normal operations, businesses can reduce unnecessary exposure without disrupting legitimate work.

4. Keep Confidential Documents Away From Unsecured Areas

Everyday office spaces can create more opportunities for information exposure than many businesses realize. Printers, conference rooms, reception desks, shared worktables, break areas, and temporary workspaces often become places where documents are placed for a few minutes and then accidentally forgotten.

Consider how often employees print payroll information, invoices, customer records, contracts, performance reviews, or internal reports during a typical week. If those documents remain in a printer tray or meeting room after the employee walks away, another person may be able to see information that was never intended for them.

Encouraging employees to collect printed material immediately and return confidential documents to secure storage can make a meaningful difference. A clean desk policy can also help, although it does not need to mean that every desk must look perfectly organized at all times. The practical goal is simply to make sure sensitive information is not left exposed when nobody is actively using it.

These habits may seem minor, but they close gaps that technology alone cannot address.

5. Train Employees to Recognize Information Security Risks

Even the best policies will have limited value if employees do not understand how to apply them in real situations. Information security training should therefore focus on the everyday choices people make while handling documents, sharing files, using email, working remotely, or disposing of records.

Useful training can cover topics such as recognizing suspicious emails, protecting passwords, handling printed documents, using approved file sharing systems, reporting lost records, and disposing of sensitive information correctly. Instead of relying entirely on long presentations filled with technical terminology, businesses can use relatable examples that reflect the situations employees actually encounter.

For instance, an employee may remember what to do when a confidential report appears on the wrong printer more easily than they remember a broad rule about information handling. Short refresher sessions throughout the year can also reinforce good habits and provide opportunities to update employees when company processes, technology, or risks change.

Security becomes much stronger when employees see it as part of their normal responsibilities rather than something handled only by the IT department.

6. Dispose of Confidential Paperwork Securely

Protecting a document while it is actively being used is only part of the information security process. Businesses also need a reliable way to handle confidential records once those documents have reached the end of their useful life, because throwing sensitive paperwork into an ordinary wastebasket or recycling container can undo the care taken during storage and use.

Documents containing customer names, employee information, account details, financial data, signatures, internal correspondence, or other sensitive material should follow a clear disposal process. Employees should know exactly where those documents belong and should not have to make individual judgments every time they finish with a record.

The appropriate process often depends on the type of information involved, the amount of paperwork being produced, and the locations where a business operates. Organizations that regularly handle confidential records may incorporate professional options such as San Jose shredding services into their broader document management procedures when secure destruction is needed for local operations.

What matters most is consistency. When every employee knows how sensitive paperwork should be handled after it is no longer required, there is less chance that confidential records will end up mixed with ordinary office waste.

7. Do Not Forget About Old Hard Drives and Electronic Devices

Confidential information does not disappear simply because it is stored digitally rather than on paper. Old laptops, desktop computers, phones, external drives, printers, servers, and other equipment may continue to contain business data even after employees have stopped using them.

This becomes particularly important when equipment is being replaced, recycled, donated, sold, or discarded. Simply deleting files does not always guarantee that stored information cannot be recovered, especially if the organization has not followed an appropriate data removal or media destruction process.

Businesses should therefore include electronic equipment in their information disposal policies rather than treating old hardware as ordinary office property. Before a device leaves company control, teams should understand what information may be stored on it and what steps are required to prevent that information from becoming accessible later.

A useful way to think about an old hard drive is to imagine it as a filing cabinet filled with documents. The format may be different, but the information inside can be just as sensitive.

8. Build Security Into Remote and Hybrid Work

Remote and hybrid work have made information more mobile than ever, which means confidential records are no longer handled only inside controlled office environments. Employees may access business information from home, carry documents between locations, print records using personal equipment, or connect to company systems through networks that the organization does not manage directly.

Businesses should provide clear guidance about how confidential information should be handled outside the office. Employees need to know whether sensitive documents may be printed at home, where physical files should be stored, how documents should be transported, which systems should be used for sharing digital files, and how records should be disposed of when they are no longer required.

Home environments can introduce unexpected risks because family members, visitors, shared devices, household recycling bins, and unsecured workspaces may all create opportunities for accidental exposure. Employees may have every intention of protecting company information, yet without clear procedures they may simply choose whatever approach seems convenient at the time.

Information security should therefore follow the employee wherever the work happens. When remote work policies address both digital and physical records, businesses can preserve flexibility without leaving obvious gaps in their protection.

9. Review Your Information Security Practices Regularly

Information security policies should evolve as the business changes. New employees join, experienced employees leave, teams adopt new software, office locations change, remote work practices develop, and regulations may introduce new requirements.

A policy that worked well several years ago may no longer reflect how information moves through the organization today. Regular reviews give businesses an opportunity to identify outdated practices before they create problems.

These reviews can include checking who has access to sensitive records, examining document retention schedules, assessing storage arrangements, reviewing disposal procedures, updating employee training, and looking closely at remote work practices. Businesses can also speak with employees who handle confidential information every day, because those people may notice practical weaknesses that are not obvious from written policies alone.

The goal is not to redesign the entire security program every few months. Instead, regular reviews allow small adjustments to be made before minor weaknesses become larger vulnerabilities.

Small Habits Can Prevent Big Information Security Problems

Protecting confidential information does not always require dramatic changes or expensive technology. In many cases, the strongest improvements begin with basic questions about how information is handled during an ordinary workday, including who can access it, where it is stored, how long it is retained, and what happens when it is no longer needed.

Think about the confidential information moving through your own workplace. Would an employee immediately know what to do with an outdated customer record, or could that document easily end up in an ordinary recycling bin. Would sensitive paperwork be removed from a printer quickly, or could it remain there until someone else notices it.

These details matter because information security is often shaped by routine behavior. Clear classification rules, sensible retention policies, controlled access, secure storage, practical employee training, and dependable disposal procedures all work together to reduce unnecessary exposure.

One forgotten document may appear insignificant when compared with sophisticated cybersecurity threats, but that document could still contain information that a customer, employee, or business partner trusted your organization to protect. Building better habits around confidential information helps make that trust part of everyday operations, rather than something businesses think about only after a problem occurs.

title.rendered: Why Southwest Florida Is Attracting Investors, Entrepreneurs, and New Residents

content.rendered:
For years, Southwest Florida was often viewed mainly as a destination for retirees, vacationers, and people looking for warm winters near the Gulf Coast.

That image still has some truth to it, but it no longer captures the full picture of what is happening across the region. Communities around Fort Myers, Naples, Cape Coral, Bonita Springs, Estero, and nearby areas are growing, and that growth is creating a much broader mix of economic activity, real estate demand, business development, and relocation interest.

What makes Southwest Florida especially interesting is that the region is attracting several groups at the same time. Investors are watching population growth and property development, entrepreneurs are looking for new markets where demand is expanding, and professionals are reconsidering where they need to live now that remote and flexible work have become more common. At the same time, families and retirees continue to relocate to the area because of the climate, access to the coast, housing options, and overall lifestyle.

That combination is creating a region that is changing quickly. The story is no longer simply about sunshine and beaches. It is increasingly about how population growth, business opportunity, real estate, infrastructure, and quality of life are coming together in one part of Florida.

Population Growth Is Expanding the Local Economy

One of the clearest reasons Southwest Florida continues to attract attention is population growth, because every new household that arrives creates additional demand across the local economy. New residents need housing, healthcare, groceries, restaurants, contractors, financial services, transportation, childcare, home maintenance, entertainment, and dozens of other services that become part of everyday life.

That kind of growth can create opportunities for businesses of very different sizes. A national retailer may see enough population density to justify opening another location, while a local entrepreneur may notice increasing demand for home services, professional consulting, healthcare support, landscaping, property management, or specialized retail. The opportunity does not always arrive in a dramatic way. Sometimes it appears gradually as neighborhoods expand and residents begin looking for services that have not yet caught up with demand.

This is where entrepreneurs often have an advantage, because they can pay close attention to what is happening at the neighborhood level. A rapidly growing community may already have plenty of restaurants but still lack certain medical services, repair businesses, childcare options, or professional services. Investors and business owners who understand these local gaps may be able to identify opportunities that are easy to miss when looking only at regional statistics.

Population growth also affects existing businesses. As communities become larger, companies that have operated locally for years may find themselves serving a very different customer base than they did a decade ago. New residents can bring different expectations, spending habits, and needs, which encourages businesses to adapt and sometimes expand.

Florida’s Business Environment Adds to the Appeal

Southwest Florida also benefits from the broader business environment that attracts companies and professionals to Florida. Taxes are only one part of that discussion, but they can influence where entrepreneurs, investors, and high earning professionals choose to live or establish operations.

Florida does not impose a personal state income tax, which can be appealing to individuals relocating from states where personal income taxes are significantly higher. Of course, that does not mean operating a business in Florida comes without taxes or expenses. Companies still need to consider corporate taxes where applicable, sales taxes, property expenses, licensing requirements, insurance, payroll, and the other costs that come with doing business.

The larger point is that entrepreneurs rarely make location decisions based on a single number. They usually look at the complete picture, including the cost of operating a business, access to customers, availability of workers, housing costs, transportation, and quality of life. Southwest Florida can be attractive because those factors overlap in ways that work for certain types of businesses, especially companies that serve local consumers, property owners, healthcare needs, tourism, professional services, and residential development.

An independent consultant, for example, may care primarily about internet reliability, airport access, housing, and lifestyle. A construction company will care more about development activity, labor, materials, and local permitting. A healthcare provider will pay closer attention to demographics, population growth, and the availability of commercial space. There is no single reason a business moves to Southwest Florida, which is exactly why the region deserves to be viewed as a collection of different local markets rather than one uniform economy.

Real Estate Remains Central to the Growth Story

It is difficult to discuss Southwest Florida without spending time on real estate, because housing and development are closely tied to the region’s growth. As more people move into the area, demand can affect existing homes, new construction, rental properties, commercial buildings, and land development.

For investors, however, population growth alone should never be treated as enough evidence to make a decision. The details matter much more. Property values, mortgage rates, insurance premiums, maintenance costs, flood exposure, homeowner association fees, and local development patterns can all change the financial picture of a property.

The same principle applies to commercial real estate. A growing population may increase demand for medical offices, restaurants, shops, professional services, and other businesses, but success still depends heavily on location and local demographics. A commercial property near a rapidly expanding residential area may offer a very different opportunity from one in a market where traffic patterns or consumer habits are changing.

This is why investors need to look beyond broad claims that Southwest Florida is growing. The better questions are more specific. Who is moving into a particular area, what type of housing is being built, how quickly are properties selling or renting, what businesses are opening nearby, and what additional costs could affect long term returns? Those questions provide a much clearer picture than regional growth statistics alone.

New Residents Create Opportunities Beyond Housing

Real estate may be one of the most visible parts of migration, but new residents affect many other industries once they settle into a community. Someone who relocates to Southwest Florida may immediately begin looking for a dentist, physician, mechanic, accountant, insurance agent, contractor, landscaper, fitness center, grocery store, or favorite restaurant.

When that pattern is repeated across thousands of households, it creates a meaningful amount of new demand. This is one reason population growth can be important for small and medium sized businesses, because a growing customer base can support services that might not have been viable several years earlier.

Healthcare is an obvious example, especially in a region with a large retiree population, but the opportunities are much broader than that. Construction, property management, home maintenance, hospitality, technology services, accounting, transportation, personal services, and local retail can all be affected by population changes.

Entrepreneurs who are considering the region should therefore look closely at how communities are changing instead of assuming that every opportunity is tied directly to tourism or real estate. Some of the most interesting business ideas may come from ordinary daily needs that have increased faster than the local supply of services.

Southwest Florida Functions as a Network of Connected Communities

Another part of the region’s appeal is that Southwest Florida does not depend on a single urban center. Fort Myers, Naples, Cape Coral, Bonita Springs, Estero, and surrounding communities each have their own character, housing patterns, business activity, and local customer bases, but they are also connected through employment, shopping, healthcare, recreation, tourism, and transportation.

This creates an interesting environment for businesses because a company does not necessarily have to rely on customers from only one city. Depending on the type of service being offered, a business may be able to reach people across several nearby communities, especially when customers are willing to travel for healthcare, professional services, shopping, dining, or specialized expertise.

Airport access strengthens those connections with the rest of the country. Southwest Florida International Airport helps make the area more practical for business owners, executives, consultants, investors, and remote professionals who need to travel regularly. For someone who runs a company serving clients in several states, living in a smaller Gulf Coast community does not necessarily mean giving up convenient access to larger business markets.

That matters more than it might seem. Entrepreneurs often want the benefits of living in a smaller or more relaxed community without feeling disconnected from clients, partners, or opportunities elsewhere. Southwest Florida can offer that balance for people whose work does not require them to be in a major downtown office every day.

Lifestyle Is Becoming Part of the Business Decision

Business decisions may be driven by numbers, but the people making those decisions still care about how their lives feel outside working hours. Housing, commute times, weather, recreation, schools, restaurants, healthcare, airport access, and the pace of daily life can all influence where professionals and entrepreneurs decide to live.

Southwest Florida has a clear lifestyle appeal because it offers warm weather, access to the Gulf Coast, outdoor activities, golf, boating, dining, and communities that can feel less intense than larger metropolitan areas. For someone who has spent years dealing with long commutes or expensive urban living, the idea of structuring work around a different lifestyle can be compelling.

However, choosing where to live within Southwest Florida requires more thought than simply deciding to move to the region. Communities can feel very different from one another, and people often need to compare housing, employment access, shopping, recreation, schools, and overall pace of life before making a decision. For professionals looking at communities between Fort Myers and Naples, choices such as moving to Estero often come down to finding the right balance between housing, convenient access to nearby employment centers, local amenities, and the kind of everyday lifestyle they want.

That lifestyle discussion has an economic side as well. Companies need people, and attracting skilled employees can become easier when a location offers more than a paycheck. A business that operates in an area where employees actually want to live may have a stronger position when recruiting people who have several options available to them.

Remote Work Has Changed Where People Can Live

Remote and hybrid work have made this lifestyle factor even more important because many professionals are no longer tied to a traditional office five days a week. Consultants, software professionals, designers, marketers, financial specialists, and business owners may be able to work with clients around the country while living somewhere that better fits their personal preferences.

This change has allowed regions like Southwest Florida to compete for residents who previously might have needed to live near a major employment center. Someone can now earn income from a company based in New York, Chicago, Atlanta, or another major city while spending most of the year in Florida.

The local economy still benefits from that relocation. Remote professionals buy or rent homes, shop locally, use healthcare services, hire contractors, visit restaurants, and participate in the community. Some eventually start local businesses or invest in property, which creates additional connections between remote work and regional economic growth.

That does not mean every remote worker will choose Southwest Florida, but it does mean the region is competing for a much broader group of residents than it once did.

Growth Comes With Costs and Challenges

It is important to keep the growth story balanced because rapid development also creates challenges. More residents can lead to heavier traffic, higher housing costs, pressure on roads and public services, and increased demand for infrastructure.

Insurance is another major consideration, especially for property owners. Florida’s exposure to hurricanes, flooding, and other weather related risks can affect the cost of owning a home, operating a business, or investing in real estate. Those expenses can significantly change the financial assumptions behind an investment.

Housing affordability is also worth watching. Strong demand can benefit property owners, but rising housing costs may create difficulties for workers who need to live near their jobs. Businesses that depend on local employees have to think about whether the people they hire can realistically afford to live in the surrounding area.

These challenges do not cancel out the region’s opportunities, but they do make careful research essential. Growth can create potential for investment and business expansion while simultaneously producing costs that investors and entrepreneurs need to understand before committing capital.

The Best Opportunities Become Clearer When You Look Locally

Southwest Florida is attracting investors, entrepreneurs, professionals, retirees, and families because several trends are happening at the same time. Population growth is creating new demand, businesses are responding to changing communities, real estate remains active, remote work has increased residential flexibility, and the region continues to offer a lifestyle that appeals to people looking for something different from larger metropolitan areas.

Still, broad regional growth tells only part of the story. The most useful insights usually appear when investors, business owners, and potential residents look closely at individual communities. They need to understand who is moving there, what is being built, which services are in demand, how property costs are changing, and what challenges could affect long term plans.

Southwest Florida is not one single market, and that may actually be one of its strengths. Naples has different characteristics from Fort Myers, Cape Coral has different development patterns from Bonita Springs, and smaller communities along the corridor can appeal to people for entirely different reasons.

For anyone considering investing, starting a business, or relocating to the region, the key is not simply recognizing that Southwest Florida is growing. It is understanding what that growth means at the local level, where demand is developing, and how a particular community fits into a larger economic and lifestyle picture. That deeper view is what turns a general growth trend into information people can actually use when deciding where to invest, build, work, or live.

title.rendered: BigHat Biosciences Raises $75M in Series C Financing

content.rendered:
BigHat Biosciences, a San Mateo, CA-based clinical-stage, AI-driven protein therapeutics platform company, closed a $75m Series C financing.

The round, which brought its total funding raised to date to $223m, was co-led by DFJ Growth & Premji Invest with participation from Catalio Capital Management, LG Technology Ventures, Sigmas Group, and existing investors including 8VC, Alexandria Venture Investments, Amgen Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Discovery Ventures, GRIDS Capital, Intermountain Ventures, Eli Lilly and Company, Merck Global Health Innovation Fund, Quadrille Capital, and Section 32.

The company intends to use the funds to grow its platform for rapid data generation to power frontier intelligence for protein design, as well as advancement of its pipeline of AI-designed therapeutics, including BHB810 and BHB299, to key clinical readouts.

Led by Peyton Greenside, co-founder and CEO, BigHat Biosciences is an AI-native biotechnology company designing and developing next-generation protein therapeutics. Its proprietary platform integrates frontier AI with autonomous, high-throughput experimentation to generate gold-standard biological data at scale, creating a continuous learning loop between molecular design and experimental validation. This integrated approach enables BigHat to rapidly design, optimize and advance differentiated therapeutics with the properties needed for clinical development.

Recent achievements include:

  • Advanced first program into the clinic: Dosed the first patient in a Phase 1 trial evaluating lead program, BHB810, a novel CDH17-directed antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) for gastric cancer and other advanced gastrointestinal tumors. BHB810 is the first clinical program from BigHat’s AI discovery platform and one of the first AI-driven biologics to reach humans.
  • Nominated second development candidate: Advanced BHB299, an avidity-driven T-cell engager designed to selectively target CEACAM6-expressing solid tumors, which is nearing completion of preclinical development. The company plans to begin human trials of BHB299 in 2027.

Beyond the two lead assets, BigHat has created a proprietary preclinical pipeline of antibody therapeutics for oncology and immunology and signed collaborations with companies including Amgen, Merck, Johnson & Johnson (J&J), AbbVie and Lilly. Since forming these collaborations.

The company had closed a $44m Series B extension in 2025.

title.rendered: Bitcoin Up or Down in 5 Minutes? 1win Markets Launches Crypto Live

content.rendered:
Willemstad, Curaçao, September 24th, 2026, PlayNewswire

1win Markets has launched Crypto Live, a new category for short-term cryptocurrency price predictions. The new format allows users to predict whether the price of major cryptocurrencies will move higher or lower over a selected period, with intervals ranging from five minutes to one day.

Crypto Live turns crypto price movements into a simple two-option prediction. Instead of trying to guess exactly where Bitcoin, Ethereum, or Solana will trade next, users choose whether the price will be Higher or Lower than it was at the beginning of the round.

At launch, Crypto Live features BTC, ETH, SOL, BNB, XRP and DOGE, with prediction rounds available across five timeframes.

How 1win’s Crypto Live works

  • Pick a coin: BTC, ETH, SOL, BNB, XRP or DOGE
  • Choose a timeframe: 5 min, 15 min, 1 hour, 4 hours, or 1 day
  • Make the call: Higher or Lower
  • Watch the price: follow the market during the round
  • Get the result: when time runs out, the closing price is compared with the price at the start of the round

For example, Bitcoin is trading at $110,000 when a five-minute round begins. A user who thinks BTC will be above that price five minutes later selects Higher. If Bitcoin finishes the round above $110,000, Higher wins; if it finishes below, Lower wins.

The same format applies across every available cryptocurrency and timeframe, with new rounds repeating throughout the day.

Crypto Live brings a faster format to 1win Markets. While many prediction markets focus on questions that can take days, weeks or even months to resolve, Crypto Live is built around decisions with near-immediate outcomes. The shortest rounds take just five minutes from the opening price to the final result.

The format also removes the need to predict an exact price target. A user doesn’t need to decide whether Bitcoin will reach $112,000 or Ethereum will hit $4,500. The question is simply about direction: will the price be higher or lower when the timer reaches zero?

With crypto trading 24/7, Crypto Live allows users to make predictions across different market conditions and time horizons — from a five-minute BTC move to where SOL, ETH or DOGE could be by the end of the day.

Additional features are planned following the initial launch, including the ability to make predictions on upcoming rounds and manage multiple active positions more easily.

Crypto Live is available as a dedicated category within 1win Markets.

About 1win

Founded in 2016, 1win is a crypto entertainment platform in the global gaming industry. Operating across Asia, Latin America, and Africa, 1win offers a wide range of entertainment products adapted to regional audiences. In 2026, 1win welcomed rapper Tyga, UFC legend Ilia Topuria, reggaeton star Nicky Jam, Olympic champion and UFC fighter Gable Steveson, and Nina Drama, UFC interviewer and content creator, as members of the 1win VIP community.

title.rendered: BaazEX Enters the Asian Trading Market With a New Approach to Online Forex Trading.

content.rendered:
Victoria, Seychelles, September 23rd, 2026, FinanceWire

Baazex Expands Its Presence in Asian Trading Markets with a Clearer Approach to Online Forex Trading.

Baazex, founded in 2019, regulated multi-asset online trading platform operated by BAZ Capital Markets Ltd, has announced its expansion into Asian markets, offering traders access to global financial markets through a platform focused on simplicity, transparency, and responsible trading.

With online trading continuing to attract growing interest across Asia, traders are increasingly looking for platforms that provide clear trading conditions, reliable technology, and access to a wide range of financial instruments. Baazex aims to meet these expectations by providing a straightforward trading experience where clients can understand costs, manage risks, and access multiple markets through one account.

Baazex was built around a simple idea: traders should know what they are paying for and understand where their funds are held. The company’s approach focuses on clear pricing, accessible trading tools, and a platform experience designed to support informed decision-making.

Operated by BAZ Capital Markets Ltd, a company registered in Seychelles under registration number 8430384-1, Baazex holds a Securities Dealer’s License SD134 issued by the Financial Services Authority (FSA) of Seychelles. The platform provides access to more than 1,000 trading instruments across six asset classes, including forex, cryptocurrencies, stocks, indices, commodities, and ETFs. 

Through a single Baazex account, traders can access different global markets without needing multiple platforms. The offer includes more than 50 forex currency pairs, including major, minor, and exotic pairs, as well as over 500 stock CFDs from international exchanges. Clients can also trade cryptocurrency markets, global indices, commodities, and ETFs through the same account infrastructure.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t64_7CALVUQ

The company’s multi-asset model is designed to give traders greater flexibility while keeping the trading process simple. No matter if you are using a mobile device, browser-based Web Trader, or Meta Trader 5, clients can choose the platform that best fits their trading preferences while maintaining access to the same account. 

A key focus of Baazex is providing clear trading conditions. The platform does not charge commissions on trades and does not apply fees for deposits or withdrawals. Trading-related costs are displayed clearly, helping clients understand the potential impact before opening a position. 

Baazex also provides access without a minimum deposit requirement, allowing clients to begin trading according to their own financial circumstances. Alongside market access, the platform includes a range of risk management features such as stop-loss orders, take-profit orders, pending orders, price alerts, mini-sized trades, and negative balance protection. These tools are designed to help traders manage their positions more effectively. 

“Our goal is to create a trading environment where clients understand their decisions, have access to reliable infrastructure, and can participate in global markets with greater confidence,” said Baazex Capital spokesperson.

Security and regulatory compliance remain important parts of Baazex operations. The company maintains segregated client accounts, meaning client funds are kept separate from company operational funds. Baazex also makes its regulatory information, legal documents, terms and conditions, and risk disclosures available publicly so clients can review important information before using its services. 

As part of its commitment to responsible trading, Baazex highlights that forex and CFDs are leveraged products that carry significant risks. While leverage can increase potential returns, it can also increase potential losses. The company encourages traders to understand how these products work, consider their financial situation, and evaluate their risk tolerance before trading. 

The expansion into Asian markets represents another step in Baazex development as the company continues to provide traders with access to international financial markets through a regulated trading environment. By combining broad market access, competitive trading conditions, and a focus on client understanding, Baazex aims to offer a more straightforward alternative for traders seeking global opportunities.

Built around the principles of clarity, security, and simplicity, Baazex focuses on providing transparent trading access and responsible trading solutions for clients worldwide.

Trading forex, contracts for difference (CFDs), cryptocurrencies, commodities, indices, and other leveraged products involve a high level of risk and may not be suitable for all investors. Leverage can result in rapid gains as well as rapid losses, and losses may exceed deposited funds in certain circumstances.

Before trading with Baazex, clients should carefully consider their investment objectives, financial situation, experience level, and risk tolerance. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

title.rendered: The IPO Supercycle David Fiszel Predicted Is Here

content.rendered:
On June 12, 2026, SpaceX went public at $135 a share and raised roughly $75 billion. The offering raised more money than all U.S. initial public offerings from the previous two calendar years combined.

Two weeks earlier, Anthropic had confirmed that it filed a confidential draft S-1. A week later, OpenAI announced that it had done the same, acknowledging the likelihood that the filing would become public: “We expect it to leak so we’re just announcing it.”

For David Fiszel, the founder and chief investment officer of Honeycomb Asset Management, those developments brought new attention to an argument he had been making about the changing relationship between public and private markets.

Some of the fastest-growing technology companies in the economy were staying private much longer than companies of earlier generations. By the time they reached public investors, much of their growth had already occurred.

The Thesis Before the IPOs Arrived

In April 2026, Fiszel raised a concern that went beyond the listing plans of any one company. He looked at what investors actually owned through the S&P 500 and compared it with the companies driving some of the fastest growth outside the index.

“There are so many terrific massive private companies that are not in the S&P 500 which are growing incredibly fast,” he said. “I am just concerned that the average investor gets left behind.”

His concern extended to the companies already inside the index.

“I am concerned that those invested passively in the market, including their retirement 401(k)s, may not realize they are owning 400 companies of the S&P 500 that will be disrupted by AI,” he said.

The figure was a rhetorical estimate, not a measured statistic, but the larger point was about where investors are getting their exposure.

For millions of Americans, an S&P 500 index fund is a core retirement investment. At the same time, many of the companies most closely associated with the current wave of artificial intelligence development have remained private through stages of growth when earlier generations of technology companies might already have been publicly traded.

Fiszel believed that gap mattered.

“It doesn’t have to be the status quo,” he said. “The companies need to take the risk that the IPO market is open and the indexes can adapt.”

Ten weeks later, SpaceX went public.

What the 2026 IPO Market Actually Looks Like

The numbers from 2026 are striking, but they need some context.

In February, Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider projected that U.S. IPO proceeds could quadruple to roughly $160 billion for the year across approximately 120 deals. As of mid-September 2026, Renaissance Capital data showed 107 IPOs having raised $145.9 billion, up 411 percent in proceeds compared with the same period in 2025.

The number of IPOs, however, had fallen 30 percent.

That makes 2026 somewhat different from a broad reopening in which large numbers of companies are returning to public markets. Much of the increase in proceeds has come from a relatively small number of very large offerings.

Snider himself offered some perspective on the scale of the rebound. He described it as closer to a return to typical issuance levels than an entirely new structural surge. On a June podcast, he noted that even roughly $700 billion in total issuance, including follow-on offerings, “scales to just about 1% of the equity market.”

The comparison with 2021 shows how much the composition of IPO activity has changed. That year, 397 IPOs raised $142.4 billion. In 2026, fewer companies have already raised more money.

That fits closely with the shift Fiszel has been describing. Companies are staying private longer and, in some cases, reaching enormous valuations before public investors can own them.

When a company first lists at a valuation approaching $2 trillion, public investors are entering at a very different point in its development than they did with many technology companies of earlier generations.

What Investors Miss When Companies Stay Private Longer

The difference becomes clearer when you compare companies that went public at very different stages of development.

Amazon went public on May 15, 1997, when it was approximately three years old. The company had annual revenue of less than $16 million, raised $54 million in its IPO, and finished its first trading day with a market capitalization of approximately $438 million.

That meant public shareholders had access to nearly all of the extraordinary growth that followed.

SpaceX entered the public market under very different circumstances. When it went public on June 12, 2026, the company was 24 years old. It had already absorbed xAI in a merger that valued the combined business at $1.25 trillion and listed it at approximately $1.77 trillion.

Its free float on the first day of trading was approximately 4 percent of shares outstanding.

That detail matters for index investors because major indices generally weight companies by free float, not total market capitalization. A very large headline valuation doesn’t necessarily translate immediately into equally large exposure for someone who owns the broader index.

The change isn’t limited to a few prominent companies.

Jay Ritter of the University of Florida, who has studied IPOs for decades, has documented the increasing age of companies entering public markets. The median company going public was six years old in 1980. By 2025, the median was 12 years old, after reaching 14 years in 2024, the highest level since 2009.

The number of publicly listed U.S. domestic companies has also declined substantially, falling from a peak of 8,090 in 1996 to 3,908 in 2025. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, has noted that 87 percent of U.S. companies with revenue above $100 million are now privately held.

Research on where companies create their value points in the same direction.

An a16z analysis published in September 2025 found that companies going public between 2014 and 2019 created more than 80 percent of their eventual market capitalization after their IPOs. For the more recent cohort it examined, more than half was created while the companies were still private.

Forge Global approached the question differently. Across 56 companies that reached unicorn status and subsequently went public between 2019 and 2025, it found median annual appreciation of 65.7 percent between reaching a $1 billion valuation and completing an IPO.

That private-market growth is what Fiszel is referring to when he says, “not everybody gets to participate in that.”

The Companies Still Waiting to Go Public

The companies following SpaceX illustrate why the issue isn’t going away.

Anthropic filed confidentially on June 1, 2026. Three days earlier, its Series H closed at a $965 billion post-money valuation, and the company reported that run-rate revenue had exceeded $47 billion. Nine months earlier, Anthropic had been valued at $183 billion.

Much of that value increase occurred before public investors had a chance to own the company.

OpenAI filed on June 8 after closing a $122 billion funding round at an $852 billion post-money valuation in March. Roughly $3 billion of the round came from individual investors through bank channels, and the company also secured inclusion in several ARK Invest ETFs, creating some avenues for individual investors to gain exposure without a traditional public listing.

OpenAI also made clear that filing didn’t necessarily mean an IPO was imminent.

“We have not decided on timing yet; it may be a while because there are things we want to do that are likely easier as a private company,” the company said.

Databricks expressed a similar concern after raising $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation in August 2026.

“We’re not just a company that wants to stay private, but right now I just think there would be too much distraction in the public market,” chief executive Ali Ghodsi said.

Those comments help explain why companies are remaining private longer. For management teams with access to substantial private capital, going public can introduce quarterly reporting requirements, greater scrutiny, and demands from a much larger group of shareholders at a time when the company may still be investing heavily in long-term growth.

Staying private can therefore be an intentional choice, not simply the result of an unreceptive IPO market.

Cerebras offers another example of how much value can accumulate before a public listing. Its October 2025 private funding round valued the company at $8.1 billion. When it priced its IPO at $185 in May 2026, its valuation had risen to approximately $56.4 billion. The shares then climbed 68 percent on their first day, bringing its market capitalization to roughly $95 billion.

Public investors participated in the first-day gain, but much of the increase from Cerebras’ earlier valuation had already occurred while the company was private.

An IPO Isn’t Automatically a Good Investment

None of this means investors should buy a company simply because it finally goes public.

The historical record makes that clear.

LPL Research examined approximately 1,500 IPOs between 1995 and 2025 and found an average one-year return of 10.4 percent. The median return, however, was negative 4.7 percent, and only 40.6 percent of those IPOs outperformed the S&P 500 during their first year.

As LPL summarized it, “The first public price is not automatically attractive just because the company is innovative.”

Recent IPOs provide their own reminders.

Klarna reached a private valuation of $45.6 billion in 2021 before a down round reduced its valuation to $6.7 billion in 2022. It eventually went public at a valuation of roughly $15.1 billion in September 2025. As of mid-September 2026, its market capitalization had fallen to $5.4 billion, roughly 65 percent below its offer price.

Figma moved sharply in the other direction when it first listed, climbing 250 percent on its first trading day, but as of mid-September 2026 it was trading about 30 percent below its $33 IPO price.

Matthew Kennedy of Renaissance Capital described the change in momentum that summer: “The second quarter was an amazing rebound in the IPO space, and then July took so much of the wind out of the sails.”

Those examples are important because Fiszel’s argument isn’t that private companies are automatically better investments or that an IPO creates an attractive entry point.

His concern is about access.

If companies are creating a larger portion of their value while privately held, investors who primarily own public-market index funds enter the picture later than they once did. Whether the price available then is attractive remains a separate investment decision.

How This Fits With Fiszel’s Own Investment Decisions

Fiszel’s argument raises an obvious question.

In August 2025, he returned the majority of Honeycomb’s client capital and liquidated most of the fund’s public equity portfolio. He wasn’t finding enough attractive investments to justify maintaining the fund’s existing exposure. In his view, the market had become increasingly frothy.

At the same time, he kept Honeycomb’s longer-duration private investments and remained personally invested in them alongside his limited partners.

At first glance, advocating for broader public access to fast-growing companies while maintaining private investments can look contradictory. Fiszel’s underlying argument, however, is about where opportunities are available and who has access to them.

He believed some of the most compelling growth was occurring in private companies while ordinary investors remained heavily exposed to a public index increasingly concentrated in a small number of established businesses. His own portfolio reflected that assessment: he reduced exposure where he struggled to find attractive investments and held longer-term positions where he still saw opportunity.

That doesn’t mean every private company will eventually produce attractive returns for public investors. Examples like Klarna and Figma make that clear. It means the timing of when companies enter public markets has changed, and that shift affects how much of their growth is available to investors without access to private markets.

What the 2026 IPOs May Change

The filings and listings of 2026 suggest that some of the largest private technology companies are at least beginning to reconsider the public market.

SpaceX has already made the transition. Anthropic and OpenAI have filed confidentially, even while leaving themselves considerable flexibility over when they might proceed. Other large private companies continue to weigh the advantages of remaining private against the access to capital, liquidity, and broader ownership that public markets can provide.

For Fiszel, that’s why the question extends beyond whether any particular IPO performs well.

The larger issue is whether public investors regain access to companies earlier in their growth, especially as index funds remain a central part of retirement investing in the United States. If companies continue waiting until they reach valuations in the hundreds of billions of dollars before listing, a significant amount of value creation can remain concentrated among private-market investors.

The IPO activity of 2026 may be beginning to change that pattern, but the numbers also show how concentrated the reopening has been. A relatively small number of enormous offerings account for much of the capital raised.

Whether that develops into a broader return to public markets is still unclear. But the question Fiszel raised earlier in the year is becoming harder to ignore: if more of America’s fastest-growing companies spend their most significant growth years outside the public market, investors who depend on public-market index funds may be arriving much later than they used to.

title.rendered: Metycle Receives $150M Credit Facility from Rivonia Road Capital

content.rendered:
Metycle, a Cologne, Germany-based global supplier of secondary copper and aluminum, secured a $150m credit facility from Rivonia Road Capital.

The financing will support eligible transactions across the full trade cycle from supplier payment through buyer settlement, enabling the company to execute larger transactions, move greater volumes of secondary metals, and expand supply to industrial buyers and smelters. It also provides a repeatable framework for financing complex physical commodity transactions with institutional private credit, enabling faster execution for suppliers, and larger, more consistent flows of specified secondary feedstock for customers.

Led by Rafael Suchan, CEO and Co-Founder, Metycle is a vertically integrated secondary metals company focused on copper and aluminum. The company trades secondary metals as principal and is building the commercial, physical, and digital infrastructure to turn fragmented scrap flows into clearly specified, traceable, and smelter-ready feedstock for industrial customers worldwide.

The company’s first SmartSorting Hub in Maasmechelen, Belgium, combines AI-enabled sorting, spectroscopy, and proprietary data infrastructure to transform mixed scrap into clearly specified, smelter-ready feedstock. The system uses sensor data to guide sorting toward buyer specifications and improve output consistency.

Metycle’s trading operations manage sourcing, risk, and execution. TrustTrack, its digital evidence layer, connects records on material identity, quality, processing, custody, and logistics to batches and trades. Each processed batch and completed transaction expands Metycle’s proprietary data set on material characteristics, processing outcomes, and trade execution to inform sourcing and sales decisions.
